title: Hackers claim millions of patient records stolen during data breach at healthcare giant McKesson
snippet: The company, which distributes medicines and medical devices to hospitals and healthcare practices across the U.S., said it was hacked and expects intermittent service degradation.
fullText:
A prolific hacking group has taken credit for last week’s cyberattack against U.S. pharmaceutical distribution giant McKesson, leading to the latest spill of highly sensitive health data by an American healthcare company in recent months.

McKesson confirmed Friday in a statement on its website that hackers broke into several of its cloud-hosted accounts earlier in the week and exfiltrated data, and that the company expected “intermittent service degradation” related to the incident. In a separate notice to customers, the company’s chief technology officer, Francisco Fraga, said the stolen data relates to its oncology & multispecialty and medical-surgical units.

The Texas-based company is one of the largest American distributors of pharmaceuticals, medicines, medical supplies, and technology to hospitals and healthcare providers across the United States, and as such handles a large amount of patient data.

The ShinyHunters hacking group — one of the most active data-extortion crews of the past two years — told TechCrunch that it hacked the company’s cloud environment by tricking several employees into granting the hackers access to McKesson’s network by using phishing and social engineering tricks, which the group is known for.

The hackers said they stole a range of personal information, such as names, addresses, and Social Security numbers, as well as protected health information, including diagnoses, medications, allergies, and patient notes. The hackers say they took millions of rows of patient data from the company’s cloud-hosted Snowflake and Salesforce environments, but that they are unsure of how many individuals are ultimately affected.

The stolen data also included McKesson employees’ information, such as home addresses.

ShinyHunters shared screenshots and a sample of the stolen data with TechCrunch, and we verified a small subset of it against public records.

Bleeping Computer, which first reported the link to the ShinyHunters hacking group, said the hackers demanded a $55 million ransom from the company in exchange for not publicly releasing the stolen files.

In a statement, McKesson spokesperson Kristina Chang said the company “continues to operate in all lines of business,” and reiterated its public statement, and noted that McKesson believes it has no ongoing unauthorized activity in its systems. The company would not answer TechCrunch’s questions about the incident, such as what the hackers demanded or how many individuals had data affected by the incident.

McKesson is the latest healthcare company or medical device maker to be targeted in a string of cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers aim to steal large amounts of sensitive medical and health data that they can use to extort the companies into paying a ransom to keep it from being published.

Last week, medical device maker Boston Scientific was hit by a cyberattack that knocked much of the company’s network offline. The cyberattack had a similar effect to an incident earlier this year at another medical device maker Stryker, in which hackers abused a company’s internal tools to remotely wipe thousands of employee devices. Abbott Laboratories and Medtronic have also experienced cyberattacks, while electronic patient records provider CareCloud and health tech company TriZetto had breaches affecting over 3 million patients each.

The ShinyHunters hackers have also taken credit for sizable data breaches at Amazon-owned One Medical and dental insurance company DentaQuest following cyberattacks on their systems.

Lorenzo Franceschi-Bicchierai contributed reporting. Updated with comment from a McKesson spokesperson.

title: Mammotion Luba 3 changed my mind about robot lawnmowers
snippet: Robot lawnmowers have long intrigued me, but I never really wanted one. After a few weeks with the Mammotion Luba 3, though, I’m sold, because this fixed my biggest issue with other models. more…
fullText:
Robot lawnmowers have long intrigued me, but I never really wanted one. After a few weeks with the Mammotion Luba 3, though, I’m sold, because this fixed my biggest issue with other models.

I’m all for smart home advancements, but a robot lawnmower was one I was never really a fan of. I like mowing my lawn, crazy as that sounds, and leaving that to a robot felt like more set up and maintain than it was going to be worth. Inevitably, though, curiosity won over. When Mammotion sent over the Luba 3 AWD mower, my attitude flipped.

The main reason for that boils down to how this mower operates. Unlike many others, which require the use of a boundary perimeter or RTK base station, the Mammotion Luba 3 operates with what’s called a “NetRTK,” which is effectively just a highly accurate satellite positioning system combined with LiDAR.

The results here really blew me away. 

	

After mapping the robot to the areas of my yard I wanted it to work on, it stayed nearly perfectly within those lines, to the point where I actually had to go back and redo the lines. Initially, I’d set up several feet of buffer zone between the mower and the fairly-busy road in front of my lawn for fear that, if the positioning shifted, the mower might risk getting run over. The first two runs showed how misplaced that fear was. It hit its lines almost perfectly, which left plenty of room for me to adjust those lines much closer to the road. There’s still a small buffer, but I now know I can trust that Luba 3 isn’t going to go rogue into the road. It’s not without hiccups. Another part of the yard with a ditch left the mower stuck a couple of times when the positioning was off by a few inches, and a tough-to-access area of the property also proved tricky. But in most cases, it goes off without a hitch.

It’s all managed through the app, where you use a virtual joystick to set up a map and the pathways the mower can use to get to various zones, including crossing over driveways or perhaps portions of your neighbor’s lawn. The same app can be used to set schedules, view progress, and even watch a first-person-view of the mower’s main camera as it runs through your yard.

Taking a step back, the initial setup is an absolute breeze. Assembly and setup took around 30 minutes, with the included tools making it easy to attach the front bumper and side covers. 

Luba 3 has a docking station in the box that just needs a power outlet in the vicinity, with a generous length of cable included. You want a fairly level location for this, but I’ve found that even my slightly uneven and unstable mulch base works well enough. I’ve only had one occasion where it didn’t fully seat for charging in several weeks of use. You do get a physical RTK base station in the box but, really, you don’t need it unless you’re in some very specific circumstances. 

Like most robot mowers, grass is cut using some fairly small blades underneath, and this also makes the whole thing feel safer. Not only is there a giant “STOP” button at the top, but the blades themselves won’t be able to do nearly as much damage as a real mower would.

The physical hardware is huge, easily 2-3x the size of a robot vacuum, and it turns heads. My dogs still go crazy every time they see this in the yard, and I always see neighbors and drivers passing by turn to look when Luba 3 is out in the front. But it’s not an eyesore either. The white finish shows all dirt and dust that’s kicked up – most of the pictures in this post are after about two weeks without a wipedown – but it’s a sensible color choice as it rejects heat. It is heavy at 41lbs, but that’s totally managable for the rare occasions where you need to move it manually.

How’s the actual mowing performance? 

Good, but not perfect.

Luba 3 thankfully cuts at up to 3.9-inches in height, which matters to me. Overly short grass is how you kill a lawn in a hot summer, so it was nice to see Mammotion offers the right amount of height to keep everything fairly healthy. Whether sending it off into a thick lawn or one that’s mostly been scorched by the heat and drought of the North Carolina summer I’ve been living in, Luba 3 gets the job done well. The cut is fairly even with only the occasional straggler blade left behind, particularly when cutting at maximum height or when running it less frequently. This benefits great from running on a regular basis rather than the “as needed” schedule you’d use with a traditional mower.

It also handles slopes like a champ, with it able to cover my steep front lawn and some other raised portions of the yard without skipping a beat. Mammotion says it can handle a slope of up to 38.6-degrees with its all-wheel-drive setup. There are a couple of spots in my lawn where I can tell there’s some dead grass from Luba’s tracks, but I’ll mostly blame that on the local conditions. In some particularly uneven parts of my lawn, I do need to go back with my push mower or weed-eater, but Luba 3 really takes the bulk of the work off of my plate – complete with stripes in the finished yard.

I do think that’s an important note to make. Mammotion’s Luba 3, and really any robot lawnmower, isn’t going to fully end your yard work. There are certain sections you’ll need to do yourself, especially with regard to weeds and edging along the sides. There are options that aim to solve this, but you’ll still inevitably need to do cleanup here and there. 

But most weeks, this cuts my mowing time from an hour or two to just a few minutes – a couple of passes along the road, checking for spots it might have missed, and then weed-eating around the driveway and fence.

As for battery life, the 0.75-acre model I’ve been testing can run for about two hours before it takes a break to recharge, but that’s largely due to the hills it has to deal with. Mammotion says that, under ideal conditions, it can run for up to 215 minutes (about 3.5 hours).

Another point in favor of its navigation, too, is that it can easily handle jumping around to different portions of the yard. Zones are easy to set up and can make it easy to mow different areas at different times, or juggle things like fences. Part of my yard is gated, so having a specific zone I can run just when the gate is open is a really handy option.

All-in-all, Mammotion really changed my mind about robot lawnmowers. Luba 3 works like a charm and addresses every complaint I thought I’d have about setup, navigation, and cutting performance. 

Really, the only tough part left is price.

Mammotion Luba 3 AWD starts at $2,399 in the US, which is not cheap. But this is also on the bleeding edge and, in a world where time is money, might be worthwhile for anyone who just can’t seem to keep up with their lawn. It saves so much time.

fullText:
Jess Weatherbed

 

is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

JBL is well known for its portable bluetooth and party speakers, but now it’s also stepping into the world of connected whole-home audio. The JBL Cove series of speakers introduced today can work independently, as a stereo pair, or linked together to form a multi-room sound system, placing the range in competition with Sonos and Bose’s new Lifestyle Ultra speakers.

There are three models in the JBL Cove series, which come in a choice of black or white color options and will be available starting September 13th. There’s the compact $229.95 Cove M1, which includes three 0.75-inch tweeters and a single 4-inch woofer, but requires a wired power source. The larger $399.95 Cove P1 has Dolby Atmos support and the added convenience of being battery-powered, with up to 14 hours of playtime, according to JBL. The $449.95 Cove X1 is the flagship model, which also needs to be plugged into a power outlet, but features four 1.25-inch tweeters and dual 4-inch woofers alongside Dolby Atmos support.

The Cove speakers connect together through Wi-Fi and can be managed through the JBL One app for controlling music streams and room groupings. Notable features include automatic self-tuning, JBL’s “AI Sound Boost” technology to prevent audio distortion at high volumes, and a “Music Follows Me” feature that transfers audio to the room you’re in without resorting to a phone, by long-pressing the Moment button on the closest speaker.

Supported services include Spotify Connect, Tidal Connect, Qobuz Connect, AirPlay 2, Google Cast, and Roon Ready. US Alexa Plus subscribers can also access the Amazon assistant through Cove speakers, including voice-activated smart home controls. Each speaker also supports Bluetooth for a direct connection with phones and tablets, and can connect with JBL’s Bar Series MK2 soundbars for an expanded home theater experience.

title: TCL’s latest NXTPAPER tablet has an 11-inch display and a questionable chip from $229
snippet: TCL has launched a new tablet using its NXTPAPER display tech, with the TCL Tab A1 NXTPAPER now available for a reasonable price, but with a questionable chipset choice. more…
fullText:
TCL has launched a new tablet using its NXTPAPER display tech, with the TCL Tab A1 NXTPAPER now available for a reasonable price, but with a questionable chipset choice.

Expanding on the existing Tab A1 line, TCL’s new 11-inch models offer NXTPAPER and non-NXTPAPER versions that share essentially the same specs and design. The only difference is that the NXTPAPER version has a matte finish to the display while also including a compatible stylus.

The TCL Tab A1 (11-inch) duo offers up an 11-inch, 2112×1320 90Hz display which has a 16:10 aspect ratio. Both tablets run Android 16 out of the box, an 8,000 mAh battery, and 6GB of RAM with 128GB of storage (and a microSD card slot). 

It’s all powered by the MediaTek Helio G100 chipset, a low-cost chip that debuted in 2024 as a very minor upgrade to the Helio G99 that launched back in 2022. It probably makes for a perfectly usable tablet, but it does seem a little underpowered, at least on the NXTPAPER version that sells for as much as $299. You probably won’t see that price often, though, as TCL is selling the Tab A1 NXTPAPER on its own website for $249, and on Amazon for $229. The non-NXTPAPER version can be had for $179 through TCL’s website or on Amazon.

title: Google Wallet for Android adds 11th digital state ID, first addition in 10 months
snippet: After a 10-month pause, Google Wallet is now rolling out support for Ohio state IDs on Android. more…
fullText:
After a 10-month pause, Google Wallet is now rolling out support for Ohio state IDs on Android.

Open the Google Wallet app, tap the ‘plus’ button next to “View more” at the bottom, IDs & personal info, and then Driver’s license or state ID. This reveals Ohio as the 12th Google Wallet option. It joins Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Georgia, Iowa, Maryland, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, and Puerto Rico.

The card design shows the Northern Cardinal, which is Ohio’s state bird.

The set-up process requires taking photos of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of your face for verification that gets sent to the OH BMV. This review can take a few minutes with a notification confirming once it’s available. You’ll also get an email confirmation from the state agency.

	

First, tap on the reader or scan your QR code: Your personal info won’t be shared yet. On your phone, review what info you want to share.

Next, review what info will be shared: Make sure you’re comfortable sharing the info they request

You don’t need to hand your phone to anyone: Your ID will be securely shared using Bluetooth, so make sure it’s on

Lastly, verify it’s you to share your info: For extra security, verify that this ID is yours using your face, fingerprint, password, or PIN

“Details” next to “Show code” lets you enable an “Activity history,” while “Driver’s License information” lists license number, date of expiry, address, and more.

IDs can be read via NFC or by having the QR code scanned. It is accepted at some airports by the TSA. Officially, you still have to carry your ID card as the one on your phone “does not replace the requirement for individuals to carry a physical card.” 

Your device must be running Android 8+ and have a screen lock, with Bluetooth and Nearby devices enabled. A state ID can be deleted from Google Wallet any time or remotely via myaccount.google.com. As a private pass, it does not get synced to the cloud and is only available on one device.

Tap Personal Info.

Scroll to “Digital ID.”

Tap Manage Digital ID.

Next to the ID or license that you want to remove, tap Delete.

Confirm that you want to delete your ID from your device and Google Account.

title: Apple’s new M6 adds feature previously exclusive to high-end chips
snippet: Apple’s next-generation M6 chip is here, debuting first in the new Mac mini. And among its powerful upgrades, M6 gets a new feature previously exclusive to higher-end chips like M5 Pro and Max. more…
fullText:
Apple’s next-generation M6 chip is here, debuting first in the new Mac mini. And among its powerful upgrades, M6 gets a new feature previously exclusive to higher-end chips like M5 Pro and Max.

Apple’s M6 has both super cores and performance cores, a first for a base chip

Apple silicon continues advancing in big ways, and this week brought the latest evidence of that: M6 and the M5 Ultra.

Both chips offer innovations in their own ways. For example, M5 Ultra offers Apple’s first quad-die architecture, and M6 is the first 2 nanometer chip.

M6 also has a Pro-level upgrade in the type of CPU cores it has. It offers 12 cores total:

2 super cores

4 performance cores

6 efficiency cores

Historically, Apple’s chips have had only two cores: performance and efficiency. But that changed with the M5 Pro and M5 Max earlier this year.

Apple rebranded its previous ‘performance’ cores as ‘super cores.’ Then added a third, brand new type of core that assumed the ‘performance’ name.

The naming is a bit confusing, but here’s the breakdown from 9to5Mac’s Chance Miller: 

The “super cores” are Apple’s most powerful CPU cores. These were previously called “performance cores,” but Apple renamed them in conjunction with the introduction of the new “performance cores.” 

The new performance cores are now the middle-tier in the M5 chip architecture, offering a balance of power efficiency and multi-threaded performance. The performance core architecture is what’s new with M5 Pro and M5 Max.

M5 Pro and Max were, until this week, the only way to get super cores and performance cores in one chip. Now the M5 Ultra and the base M6 chip offer Apple’s two most powerful CPU cores too.

Previous base chips, like the M5, only ever offered two types of cores. But with M6, users will get all three: super, performance, and efficiency.

It’s just one of the reasons why the base M6 chip is an especially exciting year-over-year upgrade.

title: How I’m using Codex and ChatGPT on my Mac
snippet: 9to5Mac is brought to you by Memoket: The Memoket Gem is an 11g AI wearable that slots beside your Apple Watch in a co-wear band. fullText:
9to5Mac is brought to you by Memoket: The Memoket Gem is an 11g AI wearable that slots beside your Apple Watch in a co-wear band. Press once to capture a conversation, and Gem connects it to what you discussed weeks ago — surfacing the earlier thread with a source link. From $179, shipping August 2026.

In 2023, early adopters were just getting to know ChatGPT and AI chatbot tech. Three years later, OpenAI’s Codex agent, now part of the ChatGPT desktop app, has brought about a similar season of learning. Here’s how I’m using ChatGPT, Codex, and more on my Mac.

The summer I turned Codex

Like a billion other people, ChatGPT has become a regular part of my tech stack. But I’m a writer, not a programmer, so Codex as an agentic coding app didn’t immediately appeal to me.

That started to change in April when Codex for Mac added Computer Use.

First, a brief history lesson. 

Back in December 2014, Ari Weinstein and friends launched a new iOS 8 app for mobile automation. Here’s my 9to5Mac coverage of Workflow’s launch, a friendlier version of OS X’s Automator made for iPhone and iPad.

In March 2017, Apple bought Workflow. Workflow gained system integration and became Apple Shortcuts with iOS 12 in 2018.

Weinstein and other Workflow veterans later left Apple to create Software Applications Incorporated. The startup previewed Sky, a modern AI assistant on the Mac, before being acquired by OpenAI.

Sky never publicly launched. Instead, Codex for Mac delivered the technology in April in the form of the Computer Use plugin. 

So excited to share that we're bringing Computer Use to Codex. Computer Use lets Codex see, click, and type into your Mac apps, with its own cursor.

It's a magical feeling to have agents using your apps in the background, and still get to use your computer at the same time. pic.twitter.com/wdgxiHAKyX

— Ari Weinstein (@AriX) April 16, 2026

Trusting an AI with using your Mac, especially in the background, requires a level of trust. I don’t know what my adoption of Codex and Computer Use would be like without the history behind it.

I just know that, for me, there was a great level of inherited trust and continuity that gave me confidence in the system.

Here’s where I admit that Workflow and Shortcuts never super clicked for me. I’ve used both systems with tools that others built, but I haven’t been a builder myself.

Codex has completely changed that, but not overnight.

ChatGPT to Codex to ChatGPT … a journey

I initially found Codex to be too intimidating and outside my comfort zone compared to ChatGPT. Now ChatGPT without Codex feels like a toy. 

I’ve mentioned before that it was actually a toy-like feature inside Codex called Pets that served as the training wheels for me. (The real Codex pets are the personal projects you hatch along the way.)

I started using Codex daily in May. The first project I started with Codex is a Mac app called Flow — because it helps my story writing flow. It’s mostly a way to monitor app releases and updates. 

In my early 9to5Mac days, I used iTunes on the Mac for this purpose. It required local (and otherwise unusable) iPhone app files. More recently, I’ve used iPhone Mirroring to check the App Store on my iPhone for app updates as part of my work routine.

Describing this “workflow” to Codex started the process of building Flow. Being able to describe every little feature and change that I wanted, as if I was messaging a colleague, made it feel natural.

Because it’s my first project and built just for me, the icon is my first initial, handwritten by me (Apple Pencil, iPad Pro, Procreate), made with Apple’s Icon Composer Mac app.

Closing the loop

Because you can iterate forever, I’ve found it’s important to “close the loop” and consider a project mostly complete.

With Flow, I’ve definitely moved to the stage where I can measure the number of my 9to5Mac posts that originate from using the tool. This is an important distinction from measuring the amount of time spent invested into building the tool itself.

But because building with Codex has been such a joy, there are naturally other projects that have followed. You can just make your own Mac apps, specific to your very particular needs.

In my case, I’ve made more modern versions of apps I’ve used for years, tailored to my specific needs, right down to very specific narrow column widths.

This is very specific, but it’s very cool to me. I have a column view for social media, and a column view for RSS, on either side of my Mac display. Both are 275 pixels wide (and made for macOS 27 Golden Gate specifically). This is much narrower than the solutions I previously used, which weren’t even optimized for macOS 26.

Using X2 and Flume, I’m able to open up a significant amount of screen real estate in the middle without overlapping windows.

Social media and RSS are also mostly passive viewing apps for me. By default, toolbar button accent colors turn gray for non-active windows. But because these apps are made for me, I’m able to express that I prefer the touch of color to stay active, just desaturate a step, adding a splash of joy to my Mac.

But wait, there’s more 

At this point, if you’re still reading, this post is probably starting to feel like the guy who just discovered going to the gym and can’t stop telling everyone about how great it makes them feel. 

For that reason, I’ll just flag a few more hobby projects that Codex has unlocked for me.

First, Better Remote. It’s on the Mac App Store. If you’re already using your Mac, it makes tvOS feel like just another Mac app. Here’s a look at the update currently in the queue.

Outside of work (and spending more time outside), iterating on Better Remote has been my main side project this summer. The project started in June.

Second, Better Battery. I adore the look of macOS 27 Golden Gate, but I can’t read the battery indicator with the percentage displayed as well.

Prior to Codex, I’d probably write a blog post as a feature request to flag the issue. Instead, I’ve been able to make my own solution — during the beta period — which others can use for free.

I’ve also been testing ChatGPT Sites with a custom domain to make sharing all of this easier. I initially thought OpenAI’s Sites feature wasn’t really for me.

Publishing Better Remote on the Mac App Store required a web presence, though, which gave me a reason to test the ChatGPT/Codex feature.

Now I’m pretty excited to see where ChatGPT Sites can go from here. OpenAI recently added shared site management tools, and there’s a big opportunity for a more defined interface — like a modern Apple iWeb.

It’s still very early days for these tools, but I find it all very promising and exciting. I haven’t had this much fun using my Mac to make things since GarageBand two decades ago.

Every day, important conversations happen in meetings, on calls, over coffee, and on the go. By the time you sit down at your desk, half the details are gone. And AI tools are only as smart as the context you feed them.

Your iPhone stops recording the moment a call comes in. Your Apple Watch can’t capture what’s happening across the table. Neither connects what was said today to a decision made three weeks ago.

Memoket Gem was built for exactly that gap. An 11g AI wearable that captures conversations with one press and connects them across time. title: Tim Cook’s parting message: Apple is in the hands of a product builder
snippet: Tim Cook’s farewell memo to Apple employees offers a glimpse at how he wants John Ternus to be seen: as a product builder with deep experience across the iPhone, Mac, AirPods, and other major hardware lines.
fullText:
On his last day as Apple CEO, Tim Cook offered a rousing endorsement of his successor: John Ternus, the company’s senior vice president of hardware engineering. In a memo to employees, Cook reminded staff that he’s “not leaving Apple,” just stepping away from the role of CEO, while declaring that “few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does.”

Ternus’ elevation to the top job suggests that Apple’s next era will see a renewed focus on hardware and product execution. Under Ternus, Apple shipped a number of notable products, most recently, the new ultra-thin iPhone Air, the lower-cost MacBook Neo, and AirPods with hearing health features. He also led the hardware engineering team across Apple’s full device lineup.

Hardware will play an important role in the AI era, not only in terms of chips, but also the devices people use to run enterprise AI. Apple this year, for instance, offered earlier releases of its new Mac models, the Mac mini and Mac Studio, compared with years past, driven by AI demand.

Cook’s memo, reported by Bloomberg and others, naturally says little about Apple’s future when it comes to AI, services, regulation, China, or the other challenges that lie ahead. Instead, Cook focuses on his gratitude for the opportunity to lead Apple and exalts the company’s culture as ultimately what matters most.

“We share a belief that what we build matters and that we have both the opportunity and the responsibility to leave the world better than we found it,” Cook wrote. He also referenced the famous Steve Jobs quote about leaving a “dent in the universe,” saying that Apple makes that possible because of “who we are and what we believe,” as well as “what we value and how we see the world.” 

Cook will remain at Apple as executive chairman and will continue to manage political relationships, including those with President Trump and the Chinese government.

On X, Cook also wrote: “Sending lots of love to the Apple community on my last day as CEO. My title changes tomorrow, but the love I have for the Apple community never will. Thank you for being a constant source of inspiration. My gratitude is endless, and I’m excited for the next chapter!”

The full memo is below (via Bloomberg):

Team,

Today is my last day as CEO of Apple. This is a moment I always knew would come one day, and yet it is still hard to believe it has arrived and I am writing these words. I love this company and the team behind it, and I couldn’t let this day pass without sending a note to you to tell you how grateful I am for the outpouring of affection you’ve sent my way, for the way you’ve shown up each and every day, and most of all, for the privilege of a lifetime serving as your leader.

The truth is, whatever there is to say about my success, I know it is all because of you. You have brought out the best in me. In all my life, I have never seen or been with such an extraordinary team of people before, and every day I get to see more examples of that.

There is something truly special about Apple. I am most proud of what an annual report could never capture. This place is proof that culture triumphs over everything. We share a belief that what we build matters and that we have both the opportunity and the responsibility to leave the world better than we found it. That purpose is part of what makes this place extraordinary. Apple helps nurture it, but I believe it lived within each of you long before you arrived here. It is what brought you to this company and what continues to drive the work you do every day.

Together, we have created something far greater than any one of us could have imagined or accomplished alone. And that’s the secret to our success. We bring out the best in each other. We lift each other up. We have made it possible to leave our “dent in the universe,” as Steve once described it, because of who we are and what we believe, because of what we value and how we see the world. How fortunate we are. How fortunate I am.

As you know, I am not leaving Apple. But I am stepping away from a role that I have loved deeply. I will miss this work in ways I can only begin to imagine, even as I remain completely at peace with my decision. I will miss leading you and being with you for every step, even as I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John. Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does and I could not be more excited for his leadership.

I hope you know how much I appreciate you and what an honor it has been to be your CEO. Most of all, I hope you will continue to be proud to be part of this remarkable place we call Apple and always give it your very best. When we bring our whole selves to this work, with care for one another and for the people we serve, there is no limit to the profound difference we can make.

I look forward to seeing you in my new role at Apple Park and around the world.

With all I have and all I am, I am always.

Yours,

Tim

title: LM Studio adds GLM-5.3-Flash to Bionic, with image support and 1M-token context
snippet: LM Studio has added Z.ai’s new GLM-5.3-Flash model to Bionic, its AI agent platform, bringing multimodal input, a 1 million-token context window, and significantly lower pricing than GLM-5.2. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
LM Studio has added Z.ai’s new GLM-5.3-Flash model to Bionic, its AI agent platform, bringing multimodal input, a 1 million-token context window, and significantly lower pricing than GLM-5.2. Here are the details.

LM Studio moves fast to add GLM-5.3-Flash to Bionic

Since its original announcement in mid-July, LM Studio has been steadily expanding the models and capabilities available in Bionic, its Mac and Windows platform for agentic tasks such as coding, research, and working with documents and files.

LM Studio Bionic can use either locally run models or cloud models hosted on US-based servers, with the latter covered by a strict zero-data-retention policy.

Shortly after launching LM Studio Bionic, the company added support for Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3. Today, the company rolled out cloud support for Z.ai’s new GLM-5.3-Flash model, which LM Studio says is up to 10 times cheaper to run than GLM-5.2.

GLM-5.3-Flash by @Zai_org, aka Ox Alpha, is now live in LM Studio Bionic!

This model surpasses GLM 5.2 in performance while being 9-10x cheaper. It also supports image input.

In Bionic, this model is served from US-based servers with ZDR enabled by default.

title: Plaud’s new AI recorder is a pair of earbuds
snippet: Plaud got its jumpstart in popularity with a view on agentic AI that centered around recording summaries for students and professionals. Now, it wants to become a full-time assistant with the Plaud One earbuds. more…
fullText:
Plaud got its jumpstart in popularity with a view on agentic AI that centered around recording summaries for students and professionals. Now, it wants to become a full-time assistant with the Plaud One earbuds.

You might be familiar with the Plaud Note Pro, and that might be just because it looks like a modern retro voice recorder. It essentially is – recorded audio gets turned into highly detailed AI summaries through the Plaud app. Over the last year or so, Plaud has implemented more features to position the app as not just a summary tool, but an assistant of sorts.

The Plaud One is the next step, starting at $249. Unlike the Note Pro, the Plaud One Explorer Edition looks and acts like a pair of earbuds. The case has a lot of the same new-age retro design cues as the Note voice recorders, and it doubles as its own sort of recorder when the earbuds aren’t in use.

It isn’t an always-listening device, but it seems to skirt the line before it becomes invasive. Plaud says users can record everything the Note can, but the earbuds can also capture online meetings. It sounds like the Plaud One earbuds can capture the audio it plays, which could circumvent the difficulty of recording a call with a third-party device.

	

The earbuds themselves have all of the expected features, like ANC and transparency mode. Plaud notes they are equipped with 12mm dynamic drivers and support LDAC audio, surprisingly. With the charging case, the battery life is stated at 36 hours. On a single charge, the earbuds can record or play audio for up to 6 hours (without ANC). The case, however, can record for up to 25 hours continuously on a charge with 21 days of standby power on the 830mAh battery.

The big thing here seems to be Plaud Agent, which runs on Plaud Intelligence. In all respects, it’s an AI agent that handles tasks using the context surrounding your recorded meetings and conversations. Plaud says the Plaud One will integrate with apps like Gmail, Google Calendar, Notion, and Slack to perform tasks. Just like another agentic AI platform, the user has the option to manage skills so it does the job right.

The Plaud One earbuds seem like a logical evolution of the Note Pro and the app itself. How it handles summaries has always been extremely helpful in my personal usage, but it can be pricey.

It sounds like Plaud One will use usage credits the same way the Note recorder does. It’s unclear whether Plaud Agent usage counts towards those credits, or if, like the previous recorders, generating summaries on recorded material is what drains your limits.

The Plaud One Explorer Edition earbuds are available for pre-order starting today. Shipments will begin in Q4 2026.

title: Here’s the likely reason the iPhone Ultra isn’t getting an Apple Pencil
snippet: A report yesterday suggested that Apple considered making a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra before deciding against it. Bloomberg suggests that there are three reasons behind this decision, one of them being a desire not to conflict with the position adopted by Steve Jobs when launching the original iPhone. However, this was almost certainly not the deciding factor … more…
fullText:
A report yesterday suggested that Apple considered making a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra before deciding against it.

Bloomberg suggests that there are three reasons behind this decision, one of them being a desire not to conflict with the position adopted by Steve Jobs when launching the original iPhone. However, this was almost certainly not the deciding factor …

The idea of a shorter Apple Pencil that could be used with the iPhone Ultra is certainly an appealing idea on the face of it. The device is essentially an iPhone that turns into an iPad mini, so giving it some of the same capabilities obviously makes a lot of sense. 

Samsung gave its Galaxy Note phablets an S-Pen stylus when the device was launched back in 2011. The thinking was that this was a device that would in part substitute for a paper notebook, and it survived for a decade with a definite fanbase before being discontinued in 2021.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman lists three reasons Apple decided against the idea in the end:

It would have made the device awkward to hold, with a Pencil on the side rather than the top

It would have conflicted with Steve’s view of a stylus being a poor substitute for a finger

It would have made unsightly marks on the display

I’m not convinced the first of these would have been a major consideration, as mounting it to the top of the device would have been an option. Although this would have required a very short design, it would still have worked well enough, I think.

I’m also not persuaded by the second. Steve’s objection was not to the fact that you could use a stylus with a smartphone, but rather that existing models required this. Designing the iPhone so that it was practical to use with a finger was the breakthrough.

In any case, Steve also famously rejected touchscreens on Macs because he felt the ergonomics were terrible, but we’re still expecting the upcoming MacBook Pro model to incorporate one, so clearly Apple isn’t afraid to contradict the positions once taken by its co-founder.

I think the third factor was the one that actually killed the idea. A folding display necessarily has a far thinner and softer surface than those of existing devices. Apple reportedly waited a long time to launch the first folding iPhone precisely because it was concerned about both the appearance and longevity of the display, and allowing an Apple Pencil to be repeatedly scraped across it would have put both at risk.

If Apple can ever solve this problem, would you want to see an Apple Pencil Mini for use with a future iPhone Ultra? Please let us know in the comments.

title: OpenAI expands free ChatGPT for Teachers to 55 school systems across 20 states

fullText:
OpenAI first launched its free ChatGPT for Teachers program in 2025. Today the company announced a vast expansion of the program, covering 55 additional school systems across 20 states.

OpenAI says the new expansion reaches more than 100,000 additional educators and staff. 

“With this new cohort, OpenAI is now working with more than 100 K–12 organizations across 30 states to provide free access and training to over 300,000 educators and staff,” the company says.

OpenAI says ChatGPT for Teachers will remain free “for verified U.S. K–12 educators through June 2028.”

Separately, the firm details a new data privacy agreement related to ChatGPT for Teachers.

Alongside this, we’re also announcing a data privacy agreement spanning 16 states, a first for the industry, that provides a common framework for districts to evaluate ChatGPT for Teachers against their student data privacy requirements, helping make responsible AI adoption simpler and more consistent across school systems.

Our work continues to be guided by the belief that AI should support learning, not shortcut it, and educators should remain in control of how AI shapes classroom experiences. In this spirit, ChatGPT for Teachers continues to be available to administrators, faculty, and educators only. 

You can learn much more about OpenAI’s ChatGPT for Teachers program here. Back in July, Anthropic started its own program for free access to Claude for educators as well.

title: Samsung Galaxy flagships are a hit in the midst of RAMageddon – why?

fullText:
As the impact of RAMageddon continues, a couple of this week’s key stories have had me thinking – is the somewhat-boring nature of Samsung’s year-over-year Galaxy flagship refreshes the exact thing making these devices a hit?

This issue of 9to5Google Weekender is a part of our newsletter that highlights the biggest Google stories with added commentary and more. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every weekend, and catch our weekday roundups too!

Outside of the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s wider new form factor, 2026 has been a pretty boring year for Samsung Galaxy devices. The Galaxy S26 series is nothing more than a chipset refresh and the Ultra’s Privacy Display, while the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Flip 8 were both refinements, the latter feeling like it’s on its last legs. Then the Galaxy S26 FE launched this week, which might as well be a poster child (right next to the Pixel 11 series) for the impacts of RAMageddon with its barely-updated package that costs more than last year.

Yet, it’s working.

	

The Galaxy S26 Ultra is, as of the latest update, the world’s most popular Android phone. A $1,300 flagship is outselling Samsung’s uber-cheap budget phones that the company’s success is built on. That’s wild, and it’s also the first time that’s ever happened. It comes alongside foldables as a whole being the one segment of the smartphone market that isn’t shrinking back right now – it’s actually growing steadily. New forecasts from the IDC this week claim that the “cheap smartphone era is over” and that price hikes are essentially never going away, and it’s just looking so bleak.

So how is Samsung actually pulling it off?

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a hit, and that’s probably in large part because not only is it new, but it directly addresses feedback from users. Thin and light, media-centric designs have been among the biggest requests from foldables right up there alongside ditching the crease – which the Fold 8 also more or less does. The Galaxy S26 Ultra manages this in far less exciting fashion. There was nothing especially new or groundbreaking about the latest Samsung flagship – Privacy Display rules, but it’s not exactly a game-changer – but it proved incredibly popular. I suspect that comes down largely to the simple fact that, if you’re looking for a new smartphone, the Galaxy S26 Ultra is an incredibly safe bet. For the millions on older Galaxy flagships, it’s a no-brainer, especially with trade-in deals thrown up on top.

The strategy is working. No one has to like it, but it is working. On that note, the other thing on my mind was an opinion post asking if Samsung is actually the problem, or if slab smartphone design as a whole has “peaked.” On the one hand, yes, smartphone design has pretty much peaked. On the other, yes, Samsung is the problem. As we’ve discussed repeatedly at this point, Samsung’s existing Galaxy design is an actual problem for users and for the future of smartphone accessories. The market is moving in a direction that Samsung’s phones are incompatible with, and Samsung’s answer to that is apparently to make changes on its highest-end designs and leave the base models stubbornly in the same place. Yes, Samsung is the problem.

But as RAMageddon continues and Samsung’s devices remain a steady rock in the turbulent market, I can’t blame anyone for going for a Galaxy flagship. Boring or not, it checks all of the boxes, and that’s really all that matters for the time being.

title: The iPhone 18 Pro Could Get a Variable-Aperture Camera, but What Does That Mean?
snippet: Photographers have wanted variable-aperture lenses for the iPhone’s cameras for years. On the eve of possibly getting them, how would that change your images?
fullText:
One of the biggest camera rumors for the iPhone 18 Pro announcement at Apple’s fall event on Sept. 9 is the addition of a variable-aperture lens on the main camera. But just what is a variable aperture, and why do photographers rhapsodize about it?

We’re already expecting price increases for the iPhone 18 Pro models (and a costly leap to the rumored foldable iPhone 18 Ultra), so can improvements to the cameras help justify the expected jump? Let’s dig into the possibility of a variable aperture and a couple of other rumored improvements.

Introducing a camera with a variable aperture

When determining which settings to use on a traditional camera, photographers refer to the “exposure triangle”: shutter speed, or how fast an image is recorded; ISO, or the sensor’s amount of light sensitivity; and aperture, the amount a physical mechanism opens to let in light.

On the iPhone, and most smartphones, shutter speed and ISO are determined automatically, unless you’re using an app that gives you manual controls.

On the iPhone 17 Pro, none of the cameras include a shutter mechanism.

Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Aperture, however, gets cut out of that equation on smartphone cameras because they feature fixed apertures – there isn’t a physical mechanism that opens and closes. For instance, every image captured with the iPhone 17 Pro’s main camera is shot at f/1.78. When you take a picture, the sensor starts and stops recording the light hitting it.

Offering more than a single aperture isn’t new in the smartphone world. The Samsung Galaxy S9 in 2018 and Galaxy S10 in 2019 had dual-aperture lenses that switched between wide open (the entire lens) and a narrow opening (about half the diameter). The Xiaomi 14 Ultra in 2024 also had a variable-aperture lens that ranged from f/1.6 to f/4. Both companies ended up abandoning the feature in successive models.

What can a variable aperture lens add to your iPhone photography?

Typically, photographers will shell out more money for their standalone cameras to buy lenses that have wider or faster apertures. For example, a 50mm f/1.8 lens is a standard “kit lens” that will do well in low light and is relatively affordable (often under $250). Moving up to a 50mm f/1.4 lens, which lets in two-thirds more light, is usually a significant jump in size, weight and cost (between $500 and $1,500 or more). But it collects more light in dark scenes, and gives a softer bokeh background when shot wide open at f/1.4.

An f/1.4 lens shot at its widest aperture can give the background a very soft, out-of-focus look to put more focus on the subject. (Photographed using a Fujifilm X-T3 and Viltrox 56mm f/1.4 lens.)Jeff Carlson/CNET

A smartphone camera is already at its widest aperture, so what’s the advantage of being able to capture images through a narrower opening that lets in less light?

It all comes down to giving the photographer more control.

In bright, well-lit scenes, shooting at a smaller aperture can lead to sharper images with a longer depth of field – objects in the distance remain in focus, great for keeping the Eiffel Tower looking crisp when your subject is standing close to the camera.

In dark situations, having the aperture wide open lets in more light. But at night, a smaller aperture can create striking starburst effects around bright light sources like streetlights. When he was reviewing the Xiaomi 14 Ultra in 2024, CNET Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon named that as one of his favorite features.

A smaller aperture creates dramatic starbursts from streetlights.

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

“By closing down the aperture, I was able to create authentic starburst effects around points of light like streetlights in exactly the same way that you would by using a narrow aperture with a mirrorless camera and lens on a tripod,” wrote Lanxon recently when speculating about Android features Apple should adopt in its iPhone 18 line. “I loved the images I captured with the phone, as they looked so much more professional than the weird amorphous blobs seen around light sources in night photos from other phones.”

A variable aperture might also have more benefits when shooting video. To control exposure, the iPhone automatically adjusts ISO. Going back to the exposure triangle, shutter speed doesn’t apply here because that’s a fixed value set by the frame rate. If the iPhone can adjust the size of the aperture, it gives video shooters a second way to adjust exposure.

It also gives them more control over depth of field, keeping more items in focus at a smaller aperture value and isolating the subject against a softer background with the aperture wide open.

What we don’t know yet is just how variable the aperture may be. Although the Galaxy S9 had a dual-aperture lens, its function was limited.

Take a look at the top camera on this Galaxy S9 Plus. You can see the aperture switching from wide to narrow.

Samsung

“The Galaxy S9 was wild. It had a mechanical aperture that you could see,” said Patrick Holland, director of content at CNET. “While the idea was impressive for 2018, it could only switch between two apertures: f/2.4 to capture sharper images, and switch to a wider f/1.5 for darker conditions to improve exposure.”

If Apple’s implementation has more range between its widest and narrowest apertures, there’s still the question of how it will be controlled – if at all. The iPhone camera system is designed to handle as much of the process automatically as possible.

I wouldn’t be surprised if, to avoid overloading most people with too many photographic options (and interface items) in the Camera app, the default mode would automatically choose an f-stop (how wide the aperture opening is). Perhaps third-party developers could add manual control.

Splitting the Pro models again

What I’m not excited about is a rumor that the variable aperture could only come to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, not the iPhone 18 Pro, which is the size I prefer.

This was taken with the iPhone 15 Pro Max’s 5x zoom camera.

Patrick Holland/CNET

This could mark a return to the situation where the Max model gets the best photographic features because the larger case has room for them. When the iPhone 15 Pro Max was announced, I gave up the chance to shoot with its exclusive 5x telephoto camera because the larger phone feels too bulky to me in daily use. The same zoom feature showed up the next year on both pro models in the iPhone 16 Pro and is used on the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, albeit at 4x zoom instead of 5x.

Larger apertures on all lenses

Another rumor reported by Macworld says the fixed apertures on the other camera lenses could be increased, letting in more light. Any faster aperture is welcome, because smartphone lenses are already so small, even if it’s a tiny increment.

Would the difference be noticeable? Perhaps only in low-light images; in my experience, the main camera on the iPhone 17 Pro often has enough light-gathering capability that the phone doesn’t need to switch into Night mode.

Larger main sensor

Of any improvements to an iPhone camera, a larger sensor is the one that would make the most difference in your everyday photography because it would capture more light and, therefore, more detail in a scene. The iPhone 17 Pro uses a 1/1.28-inch main sensor – still tiny compared to traditional cameras, but not bad for smartphones. Xiaomi’s Leica Leitzphone, which Lanxon has declared “the best, most exciting camera phone I have ever used,” has a type 1-inch sensor.

The Leitzphone’s main camera delivers much better dynamic range in a single image. That’s helped by the sensor’s large physical size and the high-quality Leica Summilux lens in front of it. 

Andrew Lanxon/CNET

If the iPhone 18 Pro models are indeed larger than the already-chunky (and I say that appreciatively) iPhone 17 Pro models, there could be enough room in the case to accommodate bigger camera components.

The bigger sensor question, which has not been rumored, is whether a Lateral Overflow Integration Capacitor sensor will appear on the next iPhone. It’s a new sensor technology that offers greater dynamic range in a single image and is found in the Leitzphone and Xiaomi 17 Ultra Leica phone, as well as this year’s Motorola Razr Ultra. Sony recently introduced that sensor (the Lytia L910) in June, so it’s possible it won’t be available in Apple-sized quantities for the iPhone 18 Pro line.

fullText:
Xiaomi spinoff brand Poco has partnered with Bose for the second year in a row for its flagship F9 Pro and Ultra phones. The F9 phones double down on amped up audio, with a light-up subwoofer built into the Ultra, along with extremely bright displays, enormous batteries, and what should be Poco’s best cameras yet.

The F9 Ultra sees the return of the Bose-branded 2.1 sound system introduced on last year’s F8 Ultra. Poco has only slightly tweaked the hardware, upgrading each of the two main speakers while using the same subwoofer as before, but has changed the structure of the subwoofer mount to include a small LED ring around it. It’s only white, with no choice of color, but can be used for call and notification lights as well as rhythmic lighting during gaming or music, unlike the extremely limited HiLight feature in the new Pixel 11 phones.

The subwoofer light is subtle unless you catch it at the right angle.

This must be the loudest phone I’ve ever tested, but quality is also genuinely pretty impressive considering the size of the speaker involved. This won’t match the quality of a good Bluetooth speaker, but it’s good enough that I’d happily rely on this for playing music in a hotel room, and it’s a definite upgrade for audio while gaming or watching TV. There are a couple of audio profiles designed by Bose, plus a full customizable EQ. New to the F9 Ultra is support for Bose’s game audio engine, which can do things like accentuate the sound of enemy footsteps in an FPS.

The 6.9-inch OLED display is the other key selling point here, and it also has a gaming element. For starters, it’s extremely bright, with what Poco says is a peak brightness of 10,000 nits. But the 185Hz refresh rate is also impressive, even if Poco says you’ll only hit that top speed during compatible games, of which there’ll be more than 20 at launch, including Clash of Clans and GTA: Liberty City Stories.

Beyond that, the F9 Ultra has a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip, up to 16GB RAM and 1TB storage, and a capacious 8,050mAh silicon-carbon battery with 100W charging. The cameras sound solid too: a 200-megapixel main camera, 50-megapixel 5x periscope, and 50-megapixel ultrawide. Poco tends to prioritize performance over photography, but it still has Xiaomi’s excellent image processing running the show, so I’d expect good results from this.

Both phones have 185Hz OLED displays with peak brightness of 10,000 nits.

The two speaker systems are different — the Pro (left) lacks a subwoofer.

The Ultra’s camera system uses Poco’s first 200-megapixel sensor.

The Pro uses the same main camera, but simpler telephoto and ultrawides.

The Ultra is joined by the F9 Pro, a similar phone that’s just a little stripped back. The Bose stereo speakers lack both the subwoofer and the notification LED, the 6.59-inch display is a little smaller but just as bright and fast, the 6,330mAh battery is smaller, and the telephoto and ultrawide cameras are worse. Interestingly, it’s powered by the 8 Elite Gen 5 V Series, a binned version of the chip with very slightly reduced performance.

The F9 Ultra starts from a flagship-level €1,099.90 (about $1,275), though is launching at a much lower early bird price of €829.90 ($960). As for the Pro, it’s €899.90 ($1,040), with a €739.90 ($860) initial offer. Both phones will get four years of OS updates and six years of security support.

Xiaomi spinoff brand Poco has partnered with Bose for the second year in a row for its flagship F9 Pro and Ultra phones. The F9 phones double down on amped up audio, with a light-up subwoofer built into the Ultra, along with extremely bright displays, enormous batteries, and what should be Poco’s best cameras yet.

The F9 Ultra sees the return of the Bose-branded 2.1 sound system introduced on last year’s F8 Ultra. title: Magna increases bet on battery swapping in India with $35M for Yuma
snippet: Magna's investment in Yuma Energy has reached $87 million as the Canadian auto supplier increases its majority stake in the Indian battery-swapping firm.
fullText:
While battery swapping has struggled to take off in much of the world, Canadian auto parts giant Magna International believes the model could work at scale in India, where millions of two- and three-wheelers and a fast-growing delivery economy create a different set of economics. 

And it’s placing that bet on Yuma Energy, a Bengaluru-based firm that operates a battery-swapping network for electric two- and three-wheelers. Yuma, which spun out of Indian mobility startup Yulu in early 2023, has completed more than 60 million swaps to date and now has about 100,000 batteries deployed across its network.

Magna is now investing another $35 million in Yuma, increasing the auto supplier’s stake from the 51% it took when the joint venture was formed, Yuma managing director Muthu Subramanian said in an interview. As a result, Yulu’s 49% stake will be diluted. Subramanian declined to disclose the new ownership split.

Yulu and Yuma are Magna’s only startup investments in India, the company confirmed to TechCrunch. In 2022, Magna committed a combined $77 million to the two businesses, with $25 million going to Yulu and $52 million to the battery-swapping joint venture.

Betting on India’s gig economy

Magna’s latest investment hinges in large part on India’s growing gig economy. 

Delivery riders can lose valuable time, and revenue, while charging their EVs. Subramanian estimates that only about 10% to 15% of vehicles used by gig workers in India are electric today, leaving considerable room for operators such as Yuma if more of those riders switch from gasoline-powered vehicles.

“With Indian gig workers’ high runtime on a daily basis, an EV makes absolute sense in terms of cost of ownership,” Subramanian told TechCrunch. “Uptime is important.”

Yuma is targeting those high-mileage riders, arguing that swapping is more practical than fast charging. A battery, Subramanian said, can be exchanged in under two minutes, while even a 20- or 30-minute fast charge takes a rider off the road and requires more space and power to serve multiple vehicles at once.

However, building that convenience is expensive, as Yuma has to keep its batteries and swapping infrastructure ready before enough riders arrive to fully utilize them. “It’s a capital-intensive business, and the unit economics will play out at scale,” Subramanian said.

Yuma is not profitable yet, though some of its older swapping stations are already EBITDA-positive, Subramanian said. The firm operates more than 400 stations with over 2,500 charging units and ended the financial year in March 2026 with about ₹1 billion (about $10.5 million) in revenue. It is targeting EBITDA break-even within the next two quarters, Subramanian told TechCrunch.

Getting there will still require Yuma to build ahead of demand. The firm plans to use the bulk of Magna’s investment to expand its swapping infrastructure and double its fleet of about 100,000 batteries over the next 12 to 18 months.

Yulu still accounts for the vast majority of Yuma’s 60 million lifetime swaps, though that dependence has started to ease as about 15% to 20% of swaps in the latest quarter came from customers other than Yulu, Subramanian told TechCrunch.

Beyond Yulu, Yuma now serves more than five fleets and has integrated its batteries with more than 10 vehicle platforms, including models from Kinetic Green, Motovolt, BGauss, and Quantum Energy. The firm expects non-Yulu customers to account for about 25% of its swaps within the next two years, Subramanian said.

Earlier this month, Yulu raised $93 million to grow its electric two-wheeler fleet. Yuma will therefore need to expand its network to keep pace with its largest customer and accommodate newer fleets using its batteries.

Yuma operates its battery-swapping network across 18 Indian cities, including Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Mumbai, and the Delhi region, as well as Jaipur, Lucknow, Indore, Coimbatore, Kochi, and Kolkata. With the fresh capital, the firm plans to expand into Chennai and Pune in the coming quarters while adding more stations in cities where it already operates.

India will remain Yuma’s focus for at least the next 12 to 18 months. However, Subramanian told TechCrunch that the firm plans to take the model overseas as part of its longer-term roadmap. Southeast Asian markets including Vietnam and Thailand, as well as parts of Africa, could be attractive because of their large two-wheeler markets, he said, though Yuma has yet to begin discussions about entering them.

Unlike operators that simply run swapping networks, Yuma designs and manufactures its own battery packs and charging units. The firm makes battery packs at its facility in Chennai and charging units in Bengaluru, giving it control over both the hardware and the network that manages them.

title: Will Apple’s ‘revamped’ Health app with AI health coach debut next month?
snippet: Earlier this year, rumors were rampant about a revamped Health app coming to iOS 26.4. Then the project was delayed, and iOS 27 came and went, and the revamp still didn’t arrive. With the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 debuting next month, it’s worth asking: will we see the features debut alongside new hardware? more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, rumors were rampant about a revamped Health app coming to iOS 26.4. Then the project was delayed, and iOS 27 came and went, and the revamp still didn’t arrive.

With the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 debuting next month, it’s worth asking: will we see the features debut alongside new hardware?

Precedence

First and foremost, it’s worth going over why it’s probable that the features will debut in September. You might think “Shouldn’t all the software be unveiled in June?” – but there’s actually some precedence here.

Low Power Mode in watchOS 9, Sleep Apnea detection in watchOS 11, and Hypertension notifications in watchOS 26 were all features that weren’t unveiled until September despite not requiring the latest hardware.

So, for those reasons – it’s incredibly likely that Apple would wait until September to unveil its latest Health app upgrades, even if they don’t necessarily require the brand new Apple Watch.

There’s still time

Prior to WWDC27, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman warned that the new Health app upgrades, dubbed Project Mulberry, might not make an appearance at the WWDC keynote. Obviously, that now ended up being the case:

The Apple Health app is getting a range of new AI features that were originally planned for a comprehensive health coach service internally dubbed “Mulberry” that was scaled back. The upgrade, which includes improved blood sugar-related tracking and the ability to use a device camera to monitor a person’s workout, is not expected to arrive in the initial release of iOS 27. Apple may also announce these at a later date than WWDC.

Does this necessarily mean that Project Mulberry will for sure debut at the September keynote? No. That said, given the past feature unveils in September and the fact that we already knew it could be released later than WWDC, a September unveil feels somewhat likely, even if it ultimately ends up debuting in iOS 27.1 in October.

Feature recap

The rumors have been a bit wishy-washy regarding this feature set, since there are tons of variables at play. One of the things you may have heard was that there’d be a standalone Health+ service with videos from doctors. However, that plan was reportedly scaled back in favor of integrating the features into the usual Health app experience.

There are two very clear things though: there’ll be an AI health coach that gives you tips on your health based on health app data, and it’ll also have the ability to use your camera to give you real-time advice on workouts and other health-related tasks. Another key part of this upgrade is a new Health app design that makes it easier to make sense of all of the data.

Beyond that, we’ll have to wait and see. I, for one, am looking forward to having a much better way of making sense of my Apple Health data.

title: Apple CarPlay gaining a new AI chatbot app before Siri AI arrives
snippet: Since iOS 26.4, Apple has supported conversational apps on CarPlay. This category includes AI chatbot apps. Siri AI joins the CarPlay party starting with iOS 27. The iPhone software update is currently in beta ahead of the official launch in September. Meanwhile, the fourth third-party AI chatbot has arrived with Apple CarPlay support: Meta AI. more…
fullText:
Since iOS 26.4, Apple has supported conversational apps on CarPlay.

This category includes AI chatbot apps. Siri AI joins the CarPlay party starting with iOS 27. The iPhone software update is currently in beta ahead of the official launch in September.

Meanwhile, the fourth third-party AI chatbot has arrived with Apple CarPlay support: Meta AI.

The latest version of Meta AI for iPhone now works with CarPlay. 

The Meta AI app joins three other third-party chatbot apps that work with CarPlay: ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Grok.

However, Meta AI on CarPlay appears to be in limited testing for now. 

While the iPhone app appears in CarPlay, launching the app may include a “Not supported” message for now.

At least for me, launching the CarPlay app says “Meta AI experience is not supported yet for your account.”

I tried trialing a Meta AI paid account to see if CarPlay was locked behind a premium account. However, the message didn’t change in the Meta AI CarPlay app. Your mileage may vary.

Anyway, it’s great to see CarPlay picking up a fourth major chatbot app — even before Siri AI officially launches for everyone. 

That’s the key benefit of CarPlay: integrating existing iPhone apps with your vehicle. You just can’t expect this amount of choice from built-in infotainment systems.

Earlier this month, Meta AI also arrived on the Mac. The desktop version is much more capable than the iPhone and iPad app.

title: OpenAI calls trade secret dispute ‘a mess of Apple’s own making’
snippet: Apple yesterday presented what it said was “shocking evidence” based on analysis of a MacBook owned by Chang Liu, a former employee who moved to OpenAI. The company is alleging that two of its former employees stole trade secrets relating to hardware design and more. The AI company hit back with its own legal filing, saying that the whole situation is “a mess of Apple’s own making” … more…
fullText:
Apple yesterday presented what it said was “shocking evidence” based on analysis of a MacBook owned by Chang Liu, a former employee who moved to OpenAI. The company is alleging that two of its former employees stole trade secrets relating to hardware design and more.

The AI company hit back with its own legal filing, saying that the whole situation is “a mess of Apple’s own making” …

The ongoing lawsuit is to determine whether Liu and Tang Tan stole confidential information acquired from their employment at Apple in order to help OpenAI develop an AI hardware device. In particular, it alleges that both engineers downloaded confidential engineering files after leaving the iPhone maker.

Apple was granted access to a MacBook belonging to Liu in order to carry out a forensic analysis to determine whether it held evidence of unlawful access to the company’s intellectual property. The firm yesterday submitted a court filing claiming it had found four “shocking” pieces of evidence backing its allegations.

In its own filing made the same day, Reuters reports that OpenAI doesn’t hold back.

Employees “can leave a company like Apple that has struggled to ⁠adopt ​AI and move to an exciting startup that builds innovative products,” ​OpenAI wrote. “Apple may not like those choices. But it cannot claim those choices are unlawful, and it cannot use its own sloppy ​procedures to blame others for its own mess.”

Specifically, it says the problems were caused by three issues:

Apple encourages employees to use personal iCloud accounts to access Apple documents

Departing employees aren’t given enough time to return company devices, transfer files back to the company, and hand over responsibilities

Former employees are contacted by their erstwhile team members for assistance after they have left, requiring them to access company information

9to5Mac’s Take

On the face of it, the evidence Apple provided yesterday does appear damning. OpenAI doesn’t seem to be denying that confidential Apple information was used by the company, but rather claiming that the iPhone maker failed to properly protect it.

However, while I’m not a lawyer, my understanding is that this could become a crucial argument – since companies can only claim information comprises a trade secret if they have taken appropriate steps to protect it. If OpenAI can show that Apple did not do so, then the AI company could prevail even if use of the information is proven.

title: Apple announces App Store price changes in four countries
snippet: Apple’s Developer blog today announced tax and price updates for apps, In-App Purchases, and subscriptions in several regions. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple’s Developer blog today announced tax and price updates for apps, In-App Purchases, and subscriptions in several regions. Here are the details.

Tax changes hit three countries starting today

In a new post on the Apple Developer blog, the company announced two rounds of tax and price updates that will be applied to apps and In-App Purchases across several App Store storefronts.

The first, starting today, changes developer proceeds to account for new or updated taxes in three countries:

Morocco: Value‑added tax (VAT) introduction of 20%

Republic of the Congo: VAT introduction of 18%

Tanzania: Digital sales tax (DST) rate increase from 2% to 3%

The second, beginning September 14, will adjust App Store prices in four countries. From the post:

Pricing for apps and In-App Purchases will be updated for Israel, Indonesia, Morocco, and the Republic of the Congo if you haven’t selected one of these storefronts as the base storefront for your app or In‑App Purchase. These updates also consider the VAT introductions listed in the tax updates section above.

If you’ve selected Israel, Indonesia, Morocco, or the Republic of the Congo as the base storefront for your app or In-App Purchase, prices on that storefront won’t change. On other storefronts, prices will be updated to maintain equalization with your chosen base price.

While Apple didn’t detail the specific price changes in its announcement, the company says that the new prices are already available in the Pricing and Availability section of App Store Connect.

Apple adds that “prices won’t change in any region if your In-App Purchase is an auto-renewable subscription,” nor on storefronts where developers manually manage prices instead of using the company’s automated equalized pricing.

The company says these adjustments are part of its routine process for accounting for changes in tax regulations and foreign exchange rates.
