title: Nvidia’s DLSS 5, explained
snippet: Lara Croft in Shadow of the Tomb Raider, with a DLSS 5 mod applied. | Screenshot by Sean Hollister / The Verge Nvidia knows that DLSS 5 left a bad first impression. In March, many gamers took one look at Resident Evil Requiem protagonist Grace Ashcroft's DLSS 5-ified face and declared it AI slop. So this week, the company's re-introducing its controversial "neural rendering" with firm messaging about how it "preserves artistic intent," "respects the rendered frame," and gives game developers full control. Now, ahead of its September 3rd launch, with an official Nvidia briefing under our belt and some hands-on time with the version that leaked onto the web, we think we finally get the picture. Here's what's going on. Is DLSS 5 AI slop? The critic … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Nvidia knows that DLSS 5 left a bad first impression. In March, many gamers took one look at Resident Evil Requiem protagonist Grace Ashcroft’s DLSS 5-ified face and declared it AI slop. So this week, the company’s re-introducing its controversial “neural rendering” with firm messaging about how it “preserves artistic intent,” “respects the rendered frame,” and gives game developers full control.

Now, ahead of its September 3rd launch, with an official Nvidia briefing under our belt and some hands-on time with the version that leaked onto the web, we think we finally get the picture. Here’s what’s going on.

Is DLSS 5 AI slop? 

The critics weren’t wrong: DLSS 5 largely is a generative AI filter for video games. Kind of like a camera filter on your phone, DLSS 5 analyzes and modifies a real-time stream of 2D images after your 3D game engine is done spitting them out. It can indeed make game characters look terrible if applied poorly, like they’ve aged 20 years in a split-second. It uses a lot of GPU power, and can easily cut framerate in half — even applied well, you could argue that existing games look better without it.

But DLSS 5 isn’t what we typically think of when we think of generative AI. It doesn’t change shapes, or hallucinate words on a sign, or place brand-new fake objects in view. Instead, it imagines light, shadow, color, and detail that make the same shapes appear differently.

Image: Nvidia

DLSS 5 can make dull, pasty characters look far more photorealistic. It can fill their hair and clothing and nearby foliage with signs of realistic light. It can ground characters and objects and clothing so they don’t look like they’re floating above video game surfaces.

Here’s an example I captured myself in Yakuza Kiwami: with DLSS on, see how contact shadows underneath each character make them seem like they’re actually standing on the ground?

(Later in this story, you should really check out how Steph Curry’s jersey casts shadows on his video game body, so it looks more like he’s wearing it.)

And unlike AI-generated photos and videos, that usually produce different results with the same prompt, Nvidia claims DLSS 5 is deterministic, so games should look the same every time.

DLSS 5 is also not one-size-fits-all. Despite what it sounds like, “DLSS 5 On” and “DLSS 5 Off” isn’t just an on-off switch. Developers (and apparently modders) can drag various sliders to change how DLSS 5 plays with color and light, and they have three different AI models to work with at launch, giving your graphics “default,” “natural” or “cinematic” looks.

Plus, developers can decide whether to apply DLSS 5 everything in a scene, just a character’s face and skin, just foliage, just silverware or furniture or even just food.

You’re saying game studios could leave character faces alone? 

Yep. The toolset can automatically cut out a mask, like in Photoshop, to isolate a character’s face and skin from everything else:

If they don’t like the automated mask, devs can cut one out themselves. That’s the little “Developer Masking” checkbox in the image above. “There’s no limit to how many masks, how many groups, they could implement,” says Nvidia’s director of real-time content technology Gabriele Leone.

Would game studios actually leave the faces alone? 

Probably not! The first game brave enough to ship with the tech is NBA 2K27, and I suspect that’s because Steph Curry actually looks a bit better with detailed skin, a uniform that doesn’t seem glued to his body, and a bit more glint in his eye. Take a look at Nvidia’s images for yourself:

That basketball, too — doesn’t it feel a bit more lifelike now most of its detail is in shadow?

But what about DLSStelle and all the other horrific AI faces I’ve seen since modders got hold of the tech?

Truly deranged. But these games are supposed to look like animation, and surely their creators would never do anything like this to them, right? Right??

“The soul and goal of GeForce is to achieve photorealism in real-time rendering,” Nvidia’s director of applied deep learning Edward Liu told journalists. And games with more realistic art styles don’t look anywhere near this bad. But even realistic games can look wrong if the sliders are set too aggressively.

What do you mean by “too aggressively?” 

I’m willing to bet that if you’ve seen the leaked DLSS 5 modifying an existing game, the unofficial DLSS 5 mod was set to its default level of around 80 percent intensity or even higher. Some creators will even pump it up to 200 percent to make the difference between “DLSS on” and “DLSS off” especially clear.

But I believe even 80 percent is far too aggressive for many existing games. It can feel like you’re artificially aging a character by weathering their skin and deepening the wrinkles and creases in their face.

To show you, I fired up Shadow of the Tomb Raider. Here’s what Lara Croft looks like with DLSS 5 at 0 percent, 80 percent, and 200 percent intensity:

She seems… weathered, no? But at 40 percent intensity, she still looks like the same video game character to me, only with a bit more life in her eyes:

Similarly, here’s Kazuma Kiryu from Yakuza Kiwami once more. In this part of the game, he’s supposed to be 27 years old, and nowhere near the grizzled veteran he is by Yakuza 6. But as I ramp up the intensity from 0 to 40 to 85 percent, you can see his furrowed brow gets more furrowed, his hair lightens, and the increased shadow across his cheeks makes his face appear slightly gaunt.

0 percent intensity (DLSS 5 off). Tap to enlarge; use arrows to compare.

40 percent intensity.

85 percent intensity.

He looks older — even if the underlying geometry of his face hasn’t actually changed. In a cutscene at 85 percent, it even looks like his hair might be tinged with grey:

But again, it’s something developers and modders can control with some granularity. I’d probably enjoy a version of DLSS 5 for older games that ignores the faces but enhances a character’s gear. Kiryu’s sworn brother and antagonist Nishiki, below, doesn’t quite look right to me — but his eyepatch and necklace look excellent.

By the way, these are just me playing with the overarching DLSS 5 slider when set to its “default” model. There are actually three different AI models, each with a slightly different look, and two different sliders, one for “tone” and one for “structure.”

What’s the difference? 

I’m telling myself that “tone” is about light and color, while “structure” is about shadows and definition. But it’s probably easier to show you by isolating each:

Officially, Nvidia says that “structure intensity” controls a mix of ambient occlusion, contact shadows, reflections and subsurface scattering (read: how light scatters through materials like hair, skin, and leaves), while “tone intensity” controls color and “broader lighting” details.

What about the three different AI models?

Nvidia only called them Model A, Model B and Model C in my briefing, but the DLSS 5 mod I used describes them as “default,” “cinematic” and “natural.” Here’s the image Nvidia provided to show the difference:

And here’s my own comparison in Shadow of the Tomb Raider — you may need to blow these up and cycle through to spot the differences.

Is this really an AI filter? It doesn’t use the game engine at all?

Nvidia says that DLSS 5 can take some cues from game engines. But it’s based on the colors and motion vectors that it sees in the flat 2D frames, after they’re rendered and after other techniques like DLSS Super Resolution are applied.

When we asked how DLSS 5 knows the difference between a character model, an object, and a piece of foliage, Liu replied that the model was trained to recognize what it sees. “Just like a person, if you look at anything, you know where things are.”

You can even technically run DLSS 5 on video capture from a Nintendo Switch 2, and modders have already found ways to inject it into earlier games that used OpenGL and DirectX 9.

Will game developers actually buy into DLSS 5? Will they use it well? 

That’s one of the big remaining questions — and one that Nvidia left unanswered during and after our briefing.

While Nvidia said in March that DLSS 5 would come to at least 16 different games including Assassin’s Creed Shadows, Hogwarts Legacy, Starfield, and Resident Evil Requiem, the company did not answer questions about when DLSS 5 might come to any game beyond NBA 2K27, nor did it confirm that other titles are still coming following the original backlash. Perhaps Nvidia and its partners will wait and see how reviewers and gamers react first.

It’s worth noting that this may be a niche technology to start: while it no longer requires two RTX 5090 GPUs to function, it still uses a lot of horsepower. Officially, DLSS 5 is only coming to the latest RTX 50 series GPUs, which have become quite expensive: even a lower-mid-range RTX 5060 retailers for around $470 these days.

Nvidia claims that an RTX 5060 is enough to play NBA 2K27 at 1080p with ultra settings, ray tracing, and DLSS 5 enabled — assuming you’re pairing it with a fast gaming CPU and a whole heap of RAM.

These framerates are with 6x frame-gen enabled, so divide by six to get a better idea of how responsive the game might feel.

Just how much of a performance hit are we talking?

With NBA 2K27, Nvidia claims the performance hit is 50 to 60 percent on average across all Nvidia RTX 50-series GPUs. When I ran the Shadow of the Tomb Raider benchmark at 1440p with on an RTX 5090 at Highest spec, DLSS Quality and an unofficial DLSS 5 mod, I saw framerate exactly cut in half — 312fps with DLSS 5 off, 156fps with it on.

Will gamers be able to tweak DLSS 5 the way they like?

The DLSS 5 mods are so easy to apply, it seems like the cat is out of the bag. But Nvidia’s message is that the developer has full control, and it didn’t answer questions about whether it’ll provide controls to gamers, too.

Which mod should I install? 

I don’t yet feel comfortable recommending one — there’s been a feeding frenzy for DLSS 5 mods ever since the leak and we haven’t been able to properly vet. I installed one on a completely fresh system, just in case something went wrong.

How have gamers reacted to Nvidia’s re-introduction of DLSS 5 so far? 

The reactions have been all over the place since DLSS 5 leaked and modders began posting their work. I’ve seen people say that DLSS 5 looks like a free next-gen remaster of any game you like, and I’ve seen people say it looks as terrible as it did before. I’ve seen people suggest that even if it looks good, it’ll make every game look too similar once developers start using it as a crutch.

But many of those impressions were based on images and videos of the tech at its extremes. Once people realize there’s granular control, perhaps reactions will become more measured.

Venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz has expanded its fifth growth fund to $8.5 billion. That means the firm added another $1.75 billion since the fund launched in January with $6.75 billion.

The firm’s announcement comes just days after a16z announced it had raised a fresh $1.1 billion for a new and different fund that it’s calling the “Machine Age Fund.” The fund’s throwback, steampunk-esque name reflects its focus on AI hardware startups developing chips, memory, networking, and storage.

As the growth fund’s name implies, it is cash dedicated to funding growth-stage startups that are ramping up products, expanding into new geographies, and scaling just about  everything else. 

Over seven years, the growth fund has invested in more than 100 companies, David George, a general partner who leads the growth investment team, wrote in his announcement blog. But in this age of AI, companies are reaching the growth stage faster and gobbling up more cash at higher valuations than ever, too.

With these billions, a16z is pursuing enterprise and consumer AI tech, defense tech, robotics, infrastructure hardware and software, and health tech — really the whole stack. In this election year, it is also spending big on politics and lobbying.

These new funds follow the $15 billion in new funding a16z announced in January. At the time, it had $90 billion of assets under management.

title: A group funded by Andreessen, Horowitz, and Brockman plans data center ads to sway midterms
snippet: Build American AI plans to lobby voters in select states about the virtues of data centers by spending millions of dollars on ads.
fullText:
A well-known, pro-AI super political action committee is behind a new group that plans to blast voters in key battleground states with ads advocating for data centers, several outlets are reporting.

That new group, called Build American AI, wants to convince citizens of the virtues of having data centers in their backyards. It says it is affiliated with Leading the Future (LTF), a super PAC heavily funded by VCs Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, along with OpenAI President Greg Brockman.

Build American AI told Bloomberg it will focus its ads on Kansas, Ohio, and Wisconsin, where concerns about data centers have become a central theme in statewide elections. It said its ad budget is millions of dollars.

LTF launched with over $50 million in funding and has mostly used that money to donate to specific politicians, Politico reports. It supports candidates who advocate for AI, but it also works to oppose candidates who lobby against the technology, sources have told Politico.

LTF has become such a well-known, and not particularly beloved, force in AI-related election politics that OpenAI publicly distanced itself from it in a blog post in June.

“There have been questions around Leading the Future (LTF), which has received support from our President and co-founder, Greg Brockman, and his wife Anna,” OpenAI wrote. “OpenAI does not direct the activities of LTF, or have visibility into their operations.”

OpenAI also condemned some of LTF’s tactics, writing: “Groups that are advocating on AI should be clear about their policy views, be honest about whom they represent, and not use tactics like astroturfing that obscure the real choices facing policymakers and the public.” (Astroturfing means making a paid, organized campaign look like grassroots support.)

While LTF has gained attention in Silicon Valley, it is not the only super PAC pushing an AI agenda that is backed by big Valley names. Anthropic, for instance, is a known supporter of Public First Action, a group that backs AI regulation.

Meanwhile, Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz have been “spending on politics like no other” as The New York Times put it. By the outlet’s calculations, their venture firm, Andreessen Horowitz, is the biggest donor so far to the midterm elections, spending more than high-profile donors like Elon Musk and George Soros. The firm has spread over $115 million around so far in disclosed federal contributions. In addition to LTF and AI causes, it is also heavily supporting pro-crypto efforts, especially through the crypto super PAC Fairshake.

title: Galaxy S27 Ultra’s major redesign detailed in new renders, price hike rumored
snippet: Samsung’s new Galaxy S27 Ultra is getting a massive redesign and, thanks to the latest leak, we’ve got a better look at what to expect, but we’re also now bracing for a major price hike. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s new Galaxy S27 Ultra is getting a massive redesign and, thanks to the latest leak, we’ve got a better look at what to expect, but we’re also now bracing for a major price hike.

Following leaks over the weekend that first depicted Samsung’s new design, @OnLeaks and Android Headlines have posted CAD-based renders of the Galaxy S27 Ultra’s new design. While these renders are never completely infallible – mistakes have been made before – the track record speaks for itself, and it’s very likely this is the device we’ll see released in January.

With that in mind, this is a pretty radical redesign on Samsung’s part, especially just months after the company insisted its vertical camera design was its “core identity.”

The new look has a camera plateau similar to the iPhone 16 series, while the overall shape of the device is mostly unchanged. It is a little bit bigger, though, with the dimensions supposedly coming in at 163.76 x 78.25 x 7.97mm – just a hair larger in every dimension compared to Galaxy S26 Ultra. The camera module bumps out to 12.53mm, apparently, which sounds wild. 

	

The S Pen also remains in place here.

	

Galaxy S27 Ultra is expected to be a pretty big upgrade, also packing a much larger battery, Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon flagship, and more, though it is losing a telephoto camera.

That might all come at a cost, though. A post on Twitter/X from @phonefuturist claims that Galaxy S27 Ultra could start at a whopping $1,499 – a $200 price hike over the current S26 Ultra. And, despite the new design, Qi2 magnets still won’t be included. That said, we’re taking this claim with a huge grain of salt, as we’re not sure of the track record of this account. Neither claim is unreasonable, though.

title: VLC crosses 7 billion downloads
snippet: In our world of expensive streaming platforms, the very free and offline VLC media player has crossed 7 billion downloads.
fullText:
In our world of expensive streaming platforms, the very free and offline VLC media player, developed by the non-profit VideoLAN, has crossed 7 billion downloads across all platforms.

Jean-Baptiste Kempf, the president and lead developer of VLC, sent this update in an email. This milestone comes almost 18 months after the app reached the 6 billion download mark in January 2025.

Kempf mentioned that the company recently ported VLC to Amazon’s new Vega OS for TVs. The company said it is also working on supporting all other platforms and codecs and that VLC is preparing for the VLC 4 release, but it is taking time in development.

Last year, VideoLAN had teased AI-powered translation and subtitles using local models, but it is not clear if those features were ever released.

title: Instagram cracking down on accounts that feature AI-generated influencers
snippet: As AI slop continues to dominate the web, Instagram is cracking down on accounts that leverage AI-generated influencers by threatening to restrict their reach. more…
fullText:
As AI slop continues to dominate the web, Instagram is cracking down on accounts that leverage AI-generated influencers by threatening to restrict their reach.

In a blog post, Instagram details that its “AI creator” label for accounts is now going to say “AI-generated profile,” better reflecting that the account is not just using AI, but that viewers are interacting with an influencer that is entirely AI-generated. 

Accounts that were using the “AI creator” label will have a chance to review the status and have it removed if it no longer fits their content. 

The bigger change, though, is that Instagram will actively crack down on accounts that don’t use the label at all if they are using “AI-generated influencers.” This includes not showing content in recommendations such as the “For You” page. 

	

Instagram explains:

For unlabeled profiles that feature an AI-generated person, creators can and should apply the label by editing their profile and toggling on AI-generated profile. The label will then begin to appear on their profile and alongside their content if their specific media doesn’t already have a label indicating that it was created or edited with AI. Creators who proactively add the AI-generated profile label will not see a change to their profile’s reach.

Adding the label or appealing the decision can reverse the impact, but this is a considerable change on Instagram’s part, especially as AI-generated content has become incredibly prevelant on both Instagram and Facebook, both Meta-operated platforms.

title: Pixel 11 Pro bug causing static sounds in recordings while using Video Boost
snippet: Google continues to improve on video quality with each new Pixel release, but a bug on the Pixel 11 Pro series causes static audio issues when using the Video Boost feature. more…
fullText:
Google continues to improve on video quality with each new Pixel release, but a bug on the Pixel 11 Pro series causes static audio issues when using the Video Boost feature.

Video Boost first launched on the Pixel 8 Pro back in 2023, delivering major improvements to video quality after adding in some powerful cloud processing. The feature works by uploading your footage to Google’s servers where advanced models can improve the quality quite drastically. It’s still a Pro-only feature, though.

On Pixel 11 devices, though, there’s a problem with static audio when using Video Boost.

Users noticed the problem last week and the reports just keep coming in. A video shared on Reddit shows the problem clearly, with static bursts every few seconds during the recording. It’s very obvious and almost sounds like a Bluetooth device that’s just at the edge of its range. Several have chimed in on the thread saying they’ve run into the exact same issue.  

	

A potential temporary fix for this seems to be clearing the cache on the Google Camera app and/or turning off Audio Zoom, but it sounds like Google is aware of the problem.

Let us know in the comments below if you’re running into these static burst noises on Pixel 11 Pro videos.

title: Adobe Photoshop adds optional ‘AI Assisted Editor’ mode for fully prompt-based image editing
snippet: Adobe today announced a beta for AI Assisted Editor, a new optional editing mode within Photoshop with a simplified, prompt-based interface for image editing. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Adobe today announced a beta for AI Assisted Editor, a new optional editing mode within Photoshop with a simplified, prompt-based interface for image editing. Here are the details.

Photoshop gets optional AI Assisted Editor

Adobe announced AI Assisted Editor, a new beta experience that replaces Photoshop’s detailed, intricate image-editing tools with a prompt-based interface and a simplified menu.

AI Assisted Editor can be accessed from a new toggle on Photoshop’s menu bar, which users can also choose to hide at any time from Settings.

		
		

Once the user enters AI Assisted Mode, they see a simplified interface with tools including:

Al Assisted Editor includes:

Prompt to Edit: Transform images using natural language prompts without complex manual editing.

Remove Background: Erase backgrounds, refine edges, and customize images in just a few clicks.

Generative Expand: Extend image dimensions and generate content that blends naturally with your composition.

Remove Tool: Eliminate unwanted objects and distractions while maintaining realistic image quality.

Generative Fill: Add, replace, or remove content using simple text prompts.

Generative Upscale: Increase image resolution while preserving sharpness and visual fidelity.

Al Markup: Annotate images to communicate edits visually and generate more precise results.

The Markup tool is particularly interesting for users who are new to image editing or for experienced users working on a rough concept or needing to quickly sketch out a tweak. With it, users can just roughly draw, or click on any region of the image, and add a natural-language instructions such as “Add more clouds,” “change this shoe,” or “Add a banner with the text ON SALE NOW.”

Adobe Firefly will then make the adjustments, and users can further tweak the results either in AI Assisted Edit mode or by continuing to the traditional Pro Editor.

Other tidbits included in today’s announcement

In addition to the new, optional AI Assisted Editor beta, Photoshop added support for prompt-based masked edits, which let users roughly select just the portion of the image they want Firefly Image 5 to edit.

Adobe says this addresses much of the criticism of the current prompt-based editor, which can occasionally reduce image quality or generate results that aren’t always globally aligned with the lighting or angle of the subject being edited.

Another new feature making its way to Photoshop today is a new non-destructive layer tool for light adjustments. That includes adjustments for Exposure, Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Whites, and Blacks, “so you get Camera Raw-level results without ever leaving your Photoshop layers workflow,” says Adobe.

One new tool that is the complete opposite of mask-based editing tools is “Prompt to Edit,” which allows the user to write a prompt to change the entire image, rather than just a segment.

For instance, a user might want to turn a day shot into a night shot, or a rainy shot into a sunny shot, and this tool lets them do exactly that.

This new tool supports FLUX 2 pro, FLUX Context Pro, Gemini 3.1 (with Nano Banana 2), Gemini 3 (with Nano Banana Pro), Gemini 2.5 (with Nano Banana), GPT Image 2, and Adobe’s own model, and it creates a new layer with two variations of the edited image.

Finally, Adobe announced two other features designed to offer users “more control, fewer interruptions:”

Dynamic Text, Shapes and Paths extends Photoshop’s Dynamic Text to any custom shape or path, allowing text to adapt automatically along curves and freeform layouts so you keep your formatting without manual rework.

Stock Panel Integration puts more than 900 million Adobe Stock assets right inside Photoshop in a dockable panel, so you can easily discover, preview, and use assets without leaving your workflow.

AI Assisted Editor is available in beta today, while the other tools will be generally available starting today.

title: Here’s how many foldable iPhones IDC expects Apple to ship in one year
snippet: As Apple reportedly gears up to announce its first foldable iPhone on September 9, Bloomberg reports that IDC has a bullish outlook on the device’s performance during its first year. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
As Apple reportedly gears up to announce its first foldable iPhone on September 9, Bloomberg reports that IDC has a bullish outlook on the device’s performance during its first year. Here are the details.

IDC bullish on iPhone Ultra first-year shipments

Next month at its “Surprise and shine” event, Apple is widely expected to announce its first book-style foldable iPhone, which rumors say could cost roughly $2,500.

Despite years-long skepticism around the category, Counterpoint Research recently forecast that book-type devices will account for 76% of global foldable smartphone shipments in 2026, up from 52% in 2025, with Apple’s entry helping drive overall market growth of 21% year over year.

Now, IDC (via Bloomberg) is out with an equally optimistic look at just how many foldable iPhones it expects Apple to ship in its first year of availability.

Bloomberg reports that, according to IDC’s senior research director, Nabila Popal, Apple is expected to “deliver more than 10 million shipments in its first year,” despite its steep price tag.

For reference, Samsung’s new Galaxy Z Fold 8, which features a passport-like aspect ratio similar to the one Apple is reportedly planning for its foldable iPhone, starts at $1,899 with 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM.

A recent Counterpoint Research report noted that while Samsung led the foldable smartphone market in 2025 with a 40% share, its share is expected to drop to 32% in 2026, with Apple projected to capture 25% of shipments in 2026 alone.

It is important to note that while Counterpoint’s projection covers only the 2026 calendar year, IDC’s estimate of more than 10 million shipments spans the foldable iPhone’s full first year of availability.

That said, both reports point to an optimistic outlook for the iPhone Ultra’s performance.

Looking ahead, IDC notes that Apple’s entry into the foldables market will help “avert a double-digit percentage decline for foldables this year,” adding that this category “will grow 12.6% this year and accelerate to an 18% increase next year.”

IDC also predicts that Apple “will eventually account for 40% of all foldable shipments in 2027.”

title: Everyone’s talking to their phones again
snippet: Good morning and happy Thursday. Today I’m donating to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library in her honor, reading about OpenAI’s incredibly powerful new AI inference chip, pretending to read Bill Gates’ 6,000-word essay about AI’s diverging futures, and actually watching this 2-hour deep dive of the upcoming Thief: The Dark Project Remastered instead. As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe. more…
fullText:
Good morning and happy Thursday. Today I’m donating to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library in her honor, reading about OpenAI’s incredibly powerful new AI inference chip, pretending to read Bill Gates’ 6,000-word essay about AI’s diverging futures, and actually watching this 2-hour deep dive of the upcoming Thief: The Dark Project Remastered instead.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column.

⭐️ Starred

Is talking the new typing? Despite a persistent trend towards resurrecting physical keyboards on smartphones, improvements to voice-to-text AI models have set up a parallel future where we hardly touch our devices at all anymore.

	

Purpose-built dictation and transcription apps have also taken off. I’ve cycled between Wispr Flow, Yaps, and Typeless on mobile, and Aqua Voice and Monologue on my Mac, and while they all have their advantages and quirks, they ultimately do the same thing. And like so many SaaS products, they run on a freemium pricing model that provides a small amount of free usage and an $8 to $12/mo fee for premium features.

Last month, OpenAI unveiled GPT-Live, a model that allows close to real-time full-duplex communication and sits on top of a multimodal LLM it can delegate tasks to. It was the latest in a long line of products focused on overhauling the reliability of voice inputs on any device with a microphone, from laptops to desktops to phones.

Now, Google has (re)entered the fray with Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, a model that promises to be faster and more accurate than GPT-Live and, if you’re a Pixel 11 owner, is already integrated into the excellent Rambler tool that’s Sherlocking many of the above products.

It can do all the things GPT-Live can, just faster. And unlike OpenAI’s, Google’s digital canvas is enormous. It wants you to talk to your Google Docs and Sheets, Gemini Live and Spark on Mac and mobile, and potentially more disruptively, through its Gemini API, by which developers can integrate voice input into their own apps.

Voice input isn’t new or novel — I’ve been sending WhatsApp voice memos to friends and family for years — but this new paradigm combines accurate transcription, where a model intelligently removes verbal tics and reformats text into tables or charts, with dynamic action. Think dictating an email that includes instructions to insert a specific photo from your camera roll and embed a map with directions. The combination of speed and dynamism is certainly enticing, but I’m not yet a complete convert.

There’s something tactile and contemplative about typing and communing directly with a thought that can’t be recreated with voice. And a world where everyone on the subway is dictating their commands to an agent sounds awful. But there’s a growing contingent of people, particularly those with fine motor impairments, who will find massive benefit from intelligent voice models, and that’s a world I’m OK with.

✉️ Inbox

Galaxy S27 Ultra’s major redesign detailed in new renders, price hike rumored. Of course the next Galaxy flagship will be more expensive, but it’ll also wobble less on a table, so it’s a fair trade-off.

Galaxy S27 leaks reveal a design that Samsung just won’t kill

Galaxy S26 Ultra is the world’s most popular Android phone, and that’s a first. The iPhone 17 is the world’s most popular phone, but Samsung’s most expensive phone that isn’t a foldable is, for the first time, the top-selling Android phone.

Nothing’s Android 17 update debuts this week with redesigns, new apps, 3D emoji [Gallery]. Nothing’s tasteful take on Android meets a bunch of really nice Android 17 features. Looking forward to this one.

Nothing starts Android 17 beta rollout, Phone (3) immediately met with error messages

Motorola details Android 17 update that you might get eventually

Galaxy Watch 8 starts getting Wear OS 7 in beta

Qualcomm’s next Snapdragon flagship chip has 5 GHz Oryon CPU. Qualcomm hasn’t revealed the manufacturing process of its latest chip, but Apple’s newly announced M6 is being built on TSMC’s 2nm fab, so it’s almost certain the Elite Gen 6 will be a fast follower.

Xiaomi’s version of the wider Galaxy Z Fold 8 shows up in hands-on leak ahead of launch. Now that Samsung’s gone and done it, and with Apple soon to debut its own, we’re seeing wide foldables from the big Chinese OEMs. 

Google Play mandating reduced memory usage & seamless device migration in 2027. As I talked about in a previous Inbox edition, thanks to the RAM crisis, Android is entering its efficiency era.

The ‘cheap smartphone era is over’ and price hikes are ‘permanent,’ bleak forecast reveals. Think prices will drop when demand for components levels out in 2028 or so? Don’t be silly.

Google Keep for Android rolls out ‘Find in note’ search. I’m still waiting for Google’s big Gemini-based Keep redesign, but I also like that the note-taking app feels like a vestige of an older, simpler time.

Our team also played with a few gadgets this week. First, Ben toyed with this weird Pebblebee tracker that fits inside a bike handle or golf club and works across iOS and Android. Then Andrew got testy about Google’s mid-quality default Fitbit Air straps. Damien compared the Pixel 11 to its predecessor, and then Ben told it like it is re: the Pixel 11 Pro Fold:

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold isn’t the best, but it’s also not bad either. Sort of like how every smartphone has a good camera now and it all comes down to your priorities and taste, the same applies to foldables. You’re checking every important box with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, but are you hitting the parts you care about most? If so, Pixel 11 Pro Fold starts at $1,899.

🍎 Upcoming

It’s been a busy week on the Apple front. First, the company unveiled new M6 and M5 Max/Ultra chips, and then the Mac Mini and Mac Studio updates powered by them. The quick takeaway is that the M6 is very efficient and the M5 Max/Ultra is almost certainly too powerful for most people, but all the new hardware comes with considerable price bumps at every tier. The most expensive M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 256GB of RAM and 16TB of storage costs a cool $18,300, but Apple promises that a 512GB version is coming in October. Any guesses on what that one will cost?

Apple then unleashed a long-anticipated change to its Maps app: ads. It’s a controversial change and one that hasn’t gone down well with users, particularly because its App Store and News+ ads are already of such low quality.

Finally, and perhaps most importantly, Apple announced a new “Surprise and shine” hardware event slated to take place on Wednesday, September 9. Of course, we’re expecting a new foldable iPhone “Ultra” alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, but what’s interesting is what’s rumored to be absent: any mention of the lower-end iPhone 18. 

Apparently Apple is keeping its fall event spendy while waiting until next spring to launch updates to its cheaper iPhones, which may include the iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and iPhone Air 2.

🎾 FWD:

The end of summer brings mixed emotions, but it’s also wonderful for a very specific reason: the US Open. I’m a huge tennis fan, and you’ll find me lounging in front of the TV at all hours of the day or night watching the Australian Open, Wimbledon, or Roland Garros, but the US Open is the best of all of them.

That’s why I was so excited to see the attention this incredible mixed doubles point between the husband-and-wife duo of Gaël Monfils and Elina Svitolina and the pairing of Henry Patten and Kateřina Siniaková has been getting. I’ve already watched it a dozen times and I’ll likely see it a dozen more.

Staying on the topic of tennis, I’ve been really enjoying this four-hour Netflix documentary about Spain’s favorite gentle giant, Rafael Nadal. And if that weren’t enough, Roger Federer has been making the rounds at this year’s pre-Open press conferences in his run-up to playing some exhibition matches, and discussed one of my favorite controversies in the sport: the death of the one-handed backhand. As someone who grew up emulating Sampras, I find its demise bittersweet, but at least we’ll always have this supercut.

🗑️ Trash

You’re likely to have seen news of Meta’s $18 billion settlement around kids’ usage of Instagram and Facebook. Paid out over the next decade or so, the agreement between Meta and most of the US states’ Attorneys General comes with binding promises of limiting how much time teenagers can spend on the platform and what types of content they’re allowed to see.

It’s good news all around for advocates of youth mental health, but some $5 billion of the total is being set aside to encourage YouTube and TikTok to implement similar restrictions. It’s a savvy outcome that Meta is using as a publicity tool, releasing a statement that will run as a print ad in the New York Times, Washington Post, and Los Angeles Times.

It will be interesting to see whether Google and ByteDance will rise to the occasion (or bait, depending on how it’s framed), but either way, the scrutiny on social media’s effects on young people isn’t going away anytime soon.

Like what you just read? Subscribe to Inbox today and get it in your email every Tuesday and Thursday morning. Got feedback? Send us an email.

You can also support us by becoming a 9to5Google Pro member, starting at just $5/month. You get bonus podcast episodes, access to our members-only Discord server, and lots more.

Thanks for reading, and have a great weekend.

title: iPhone 18 Pro: Three reasons you might want to upgrade from iPhone 17 Pro
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro will be unveiled next week, and while most iPhone 17 Pro owners won’t upgrade so soon, for those considering a new iPhone there are three main features likely to motivate them. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro will be unveiled next week, and while most iPhone 17 Pro owners won’t upgrade so soon, for those considering a new iPhone there are three main features likely to motivate them.

#1: Maxed out battery life

Better battery life is often at the top of iPhone users’ feature wishlists. Who doesn’t want an iPhone that lasts longer between charges?

Last year’s iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max brought big improvements in this area, but rumors indicate Apple will push battery life even further this year.

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are expected to benefit from efficiency gains in multiple areas: an LTPO+ display, 2nm process for the A20 Pro chip, and possibly an Apple-designed C2 cellular modem.

Beyond these improvements, recent leaks point to larger physical batteries in this year’s Pro models, especially iPhone 18 Pro Max.

#2: Big camera improvements

Mark Gurman says that iPhone 18 Pro will bring “the biggest leap in camera hardware” in years.

Rumors indicate the Main and Telephoto cameras will be Apple’s primary focus, with a new variable aperture feature coming to the former and a larger aperture for the latter.

Weibo leaker Fixed Focus Digital also recently said that iPhone 18 Pro’s camera plateau will be 2mm thicker than last year due to an “enlarged main camera module.” This is another hint at big changes coming.

It would be nice to have more specific details at this point, but all signs point to Apple preparing some especially noteworthy camera upgrades.

#3: Revised design

For most people considering a year-over-year iPhone upgrade, design matters. If the new iPhone looks basically identical to your current model, the idea of upgrading is automatically less compelling.

While Apple isn’t expected to overhaul iPhone 17 Pro’s look and feel, it does reportedly have three design updates coming for iPhone 18 Pro:

New color options

Smaller Dynamic Island

Unified rear glass and aluminum

Current rumors point to Dark Cherry, Light Blue, and Silver color options—possibly Black/Space Gray too.

iPhone 18 Pro’s Dynamic Island is expected to shrink about 35% compared to the previous design, for a modern look and more useable screen space.

Finally, last year’s polarizing two-tone rear color scheme should give way to a more uniform look on iPhone 18 Pro.

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra finally dies in bend test, unlike past models [Video]
snippet: Despite their increasingly-thin designs, Samsung’s foldables have held up well to torture tests that include more bending than you’d ever see in real life. But it seems the Galaxy Z Fold 8 UItra might finally be too thin, as it’s the first mainstream Samsung foldable that’s died in a bend test. more…
fullText:
Despite their increasingly-thin designs, Samsung’s foldables have held up well to torture tests that include more bending than you’d ever see in real life. But it seems the Galaxy Z Fold 8 UItra might finally be too thin, as it’s the first mainstream Samsung foldable that’s died in a bend test.

The Galaxy Z Fold 7 showed that, yes, Samsung could actually make a thin foldable. And for good measure, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra pushes that a step further with another slight reduction in thickness. 

In the usual torture test from YouTube channel JerryRigEverything, the Fold 8 Ultra holds up just about as well as anyone would expect. Durable outer display, easily scratching inside, and some deeply unsettling crunching noises when dust gets into the hinge. But it’s the bend test that’s out of the ordinary here.

Save for the very-limited Galaxy Z TriFold, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is the first of Samsung’s foldables to break during a bend test. It’s no spectacular failure, though. The hinge and frame both stay intact; the inner display just… dies.

	

It’s interesting that the Ultra fails here despite the wider Fold 8 living through the same bend test.

title: iPhone 18 Pro is coming: Here’s what’s new with each model
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro will be unveiled next week on September 9, with new Pro and Pro Max models debuting. Here’s what rumors say is new with each model. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro will be unveiled next week on September 9, with new Pro and Pro Max models debuting. Here’s what rumors say is new with each model.

iPhone 18 Pro: Upgrades in performance, cameras, design, and battery life

Apple’s flagship iPhone 18 Pro will have the same 6.3-inch size as last year’s model, and focus on key improvements that many users care about most: performance, cameras, design, and battery life.

Performance: A20 Pro is Apple’s new chip that will make the iPhone more powerful than ever, and hit at just the right time for Siri AI in iOS 27. It’s part of the same family of chips as the just-unveiled M6, which points to big upgrades coming.

Cameras: The iPhone’s camera system is set for a big year too. The Main camera is reportedly getting a whole new module that will make the plateau thicker than ever, and a variable aperture feature either on Pro Max or both models. Telephoto performance will improve thanks to a wider aperture for better low-light photos. And there’s reportedly a redesigned Camera Control coming.

Design: iPhone 18 Pro will look a lot like its predecessor, with some key enhancements. The Dynamic Island cutout is shrinking by about 35%, the rear of the device will have a more unified color blend between glass and aluminum, and new flagship colors are coming—including a dark cherry/burgundy.

Battery: Due to the efficiency gains of A20 Pro, and also a new C2 Apple modem, battery life on iPhone 18 Pro should be better than ever. There will also be a slightly larger battery.

iPhone 18 Pro Max: Everything above, plus more

iPhone 18 Pro Max will feature everything listed above, except in a larger 6.9-inch form factor. And it is rumored to have at least one exclusive advantage, possibly two:

Larger battery gains than iPhone 18 Pro

Exclusive camera feature, possibly variable aperture

Apple’s Pro Max models always pack more battery life than the smaller Pro. But rumors indicate iPhone 18 Pro Max could extend its lead in that department.

Regulatory leaks point to iPhone 18 Pro Max having about a 10% larger battery than iPhone 17 Pro Max. Combined with efficiency gains in Apple silicon, Pro Max will more than ever be the go-to model for maximum battery life.

Additionally, a new variable aperture camera feature could be exclusive to iPhone 18 Pro Max. We’ve seen conflicting reports on whether the feature will be available in both models or not. But in his latest newsletter, Mark Gurman specifically mentioned the Pro Max model as getting it.

Will you upgrade to iPhone 18 Pro, or do you plan to skip it? Let us know in the comments.

title: Apple says these three things can speed up the new Spotlight indexing
snippet: Apple has published a new support document explaining how Spotlight indexing works across its devices, including three things it says can help the process finish more quickly. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple has published a new support document explaining how Spotlight indexing works across its devices, including three things it says can help the process finish more quickly. Here are the details.

How to speed up the new Spotlight’s indexing process

As Apple gears up to release iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, and other operating systems announced during this year’s WWDC, the company has published a new support document with tips to speed up the indexing process.

Essentially, this new indexing process creates and continuously maintains a searchable catalog of the information stored on the device, allowing Spotlight and the new Siri AI to quickly surface apps, files, messages, photos, contacts, settings, and other content when the user performs a search.

The index is stored locally on each device, which means that the process must be completed separately on every Apple device the user owns.

Interestingly, Apple had already started laying the groundwork for this change with iOS 26.6. As we reported last month, Apple said that the update would “optimize the Spotlight index to prepare for iOS 27,” effectively moving some of the indexing work ahead of the major software release.

Now, the company has published a support article with useful tips to speed up indexing, particularly the initial process, which can take time for users with large amounts of data.

Here’s Apple:

Depending on the amount of data on your device, Spotlight indexing can take hours or even days. Incremental updates after that are much faster. Indexing completes more quickly when:

Your device is not in use.

Your device is connected to power.

Your device is connected to the internet via Wi-Fi or Ethernet, in case email or other data needs to be downloaded for indexing.

Apple adds that Mac users can check indexing progress through an indicator at the top of the Spotlight or Siri window after pressing Command-Space. On the iPhone, iPad, and other devices, users may instead see a notification in the Settings app indicating that Search and Siri are still optimizing.

Apple also notes that Mail can display a separate notification when email indexing has not yet finished.

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

If you lose track of things you’d like to reference later, Laytr might be a nice solution for you. All of us save things all over the place, whether that be browser bookmarks, built-in bookmarking features within apps, taking a screenshot to hopefully find later, or just leaving a tab open and hoping we find it again later. Laytr aims to be a nice all-in-one solution for keeping track of your digital bookmarks.

Highlights

Laytr offers an incredibly organized UI for keeping tabs on everything. It works with the native iOS share sheet, so when you find something, just hit share and click on Laytr. After that, you can set what to categorize it as, as well as when you want to be reminded again.

Within the app, there are three core tabs. The first one is the Now tab, where it highlights things you need to see imminently. There’s Timeline, which lets you scroll ahead and see things based on the date you set the reminder for, and Library, where you can see everything you’ve ever saved, both in categories or grouped together. Beyond that, you can also search.

One differentiating feature is that there’s no sync, even with iCloud, and no accounts. Everything lives on your device in its own separate bubble, and your data will never live on someone else’s server.

Download the app

Laytr is available for free on the App Store for iPhone models running iOS 17 and later. You can use the app for free, but for unlimited access you’ll need a $1.99/month or $14.99/year subscription. There’s also a discount on lifetime, which normally fetches $39.99 but can be had for just $24.99 for early adopters.

Features like searching and exporting will never be limited by the paywall, so even if you decide to unsubscribe later, the app will remain usable.

title: Dropbox breach seemingly caused by egregious authentication failure
snippet: Multiple Dropbox users have been emailed by the cloud storage company to advise them that a security breach saw unauthorised access to their account. The root cause appears to be a lack of authentication by Dropbox when attackers created a single sign-on option through a third-party company … more…
fullText:
Multiple Dropbox users have been emailed by the cloud storage company to advise them that a security breach saw unauthorised access to their account.

The root cause appears to be a lack of authentication by Dropbox when attackers created a single sign-on option through a third-party company … 

Developer Yoni Levy posted a copy of the email he received on X.

We are writing to let you know that we’ve observed unauthorized access to your Dropbox account between August 4 and August 21, 2026. While our logs show no evidence that your files were viewed or downloaded, we want to share with you what happened, what we are doing about it, and what additional steps you can take.

Other Dropbox users reported receiving the same email in which the company said it resulted from a problem with a single sign-on (SSO) option using Lenovo IDs.

Dropbox partners with Lenovo as an identity provider so that users can log in to their Dropbox accounts using verified Lenovo IDs. While you may not have an existing Lenovo ID, our investigation determined that an issue with Lenovo’s email verification process allowed an unauthorized party to register a Lenovo ID using your email address and then use that Lenovo ID to log into the Dropbox account associated with that email address.

However, while Dropbox claims the flaw was in Lenovo’s email verification process, the bigger issue appears to be that Dropbox itself did not require users to use their existing login to verify the new SSO, as The CyberSec Guru reports.

Recon/selection: The attacker compiles target email addresses (breach corpora, LinkedIn, customer lists — email addresses are effectively public data).

Rogue IdP enrollment: The attacker registers a Lenovo ID as victim@example.com. No inbox access is needed because Lenovo’s verification step is missing or bypassable. The display name is set to something disposable — one victim who reclaimed the rogue account found the name “John Madden,” the late NFL broadcaster, a strong tell of bulk, low-effort registration.

Federated sign-in: The attacker clicks “Continue with Lenovo” on Dropbox. Lenovo’s authorization server issues a token whose email claim matches the victim’s Dropbox account.

Implicit account linking: Dropbox resolves the email claim to the existing account and mints a session. No password prompt, no step-up, no “link this new identity?” consent. From Dropbox’s perspective, a trusted IdP had already vouched for the address.

9to5Mac’s Take

While there was certainly a failure to verify email addresses at the Lenovo end, it would not have done any harm if Dropbox had authenticated the linked ID before it could be used to sign in. Failing to do so is an egregious fault.

The company has now fixed the flaw and expired all sessions previously ‘authenticated’ through a Lenovo ID.

title: HomeKit Weekly: Linkind’s Smart Light Stick brings flame effects with Matter support
snippet: “Flame effects” is not something I’d used before in a smart bulb, so this was a super interesting concept to me. Linkind’s Smart Light Stick aims to bring the idea of a “live flame” to a smart bulb, and it works with Apple Home out of the box thanks to Matter. more…
fullText:
“Flame effects” is not something I’d used before in a smart bulb, so this was a super interesting concept to me. Linkind’s Smart Light Stick aims to bring the idea of a “live flame” to a smart bulb, and it works with Apple Home out of the box thanks to Matter.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The Light Stick is an E26 bulb, so it screws into a standard light socket, just like any other bulb in your lamp or ceiling fan. The pitch for the Linkind Smart Light Stick here isn’t just “another color bulb.” It’s a bulb built specifically around dynamic lighting effects, with flame simulation as the main feature.

The flame effects

Instead of a single flicker pattern, Linkind lets you independently adjust flame size, brightness, flicker speed, and motion type.  You can dial it down to something closer to soft candlelight, or push it toward a more intense, fiery look, depending on the room and the mood you’re aiming for.

Beyond flame effects, the bulb ships with more than 120 presets, including sunset glows, lava-inspired motion, and Christmas scenes. I kinda always take preset counts with a grain of salt, since these numbers are often padded with minor variations to inflate them, but the range described here at least covers many of your most varied use cases rather than just 120 shades of slightly different color effects.

Where Apple Home fits in

The bulb works with Amazon Alexa, Apple Home, and Google Home via Matter. That gets you the core functionality, on and off, brightness, and color in the Home app, alongside the rest of your Apple Home gear.

It’s worth being clear about what Matter does and doesn’t cover here, though. The deeper customization options, like the flame control, will live in Linkind’s own AiDot app rather than being fully exposed through Apple Home’s interface. That’s not the fault of Linkind, but rather the limitations of this category of Matter accessory at the moment. You get basic on/off control and automation integration through Apple Home, and you use the manufacturer’s app to actually design a scene.

Wrap up on the Linkind Smart Light Stick

If you just want a bulb that turns on and off via Apple Home, this is overkill; you can spend less elsewhere. If you want a genuinely cool light for a lamp or accent fixture, something that can go from a calm living room light to a full flame effect for a party, the Light Stick is one of the more feature-rich options I’ve seen, and the Matter support means it won’t be siloed away from the rest of your smart home.

You can grab it from Amazon.

title: Google Play mandating reduced memory usage & seamless device migration in 2027
snippet: In response to the “significant hardware supply constraints that are altering device memory availability,” Google aims to reduce the memory usage of Android apps. more…
fullText:
In response to the “significant hardware supply constraints that are altering device memory availability,” Google aims to reduce the memory usage of Android apps.

On Android 17, this involves per-app memory limits that are first available on Pixel devices but will soon be adopted by an “increasing number of manufacturers.” Applications that exceed these limits “will be slowed down and may be terminated.”

Meanwhile, Google Play is establishing performance thresholds across three areas:

Dynamic memory usage (anonymous RSS + swap): This tracks the memory used for your app’s private data storage, including both active and compressed memory. It excludes files stored on the device, such as code or assets. We will assess this usage across different app states (like when your app is in use or running in the background) and device performance categories.

Bitmap memory usage: This evaluates the memory consumed by bitmaps. While bitmaps occupy memory when your app is in the foreground, they should not be held in memory for extended periods of time in non-visible app states such as background and cached.

Optimized DEX code:  A well-optimized Android App Bundle uses less memory, starts faster, reduces ANRs, and improves rendering and runtime performance. To ensure an optimized footprint, apps published on Google Play apps published on Google Play must be optimized with a minimum of 25% coverage across optimization, shrinking, and obfuscation using a tool such as R8 or any other shrinking tool.     

Memory enforcement starts in February 2027, with Google offering several Play Console tools and metrics. Apps and games that don’t meet these thresholds “will see reduced app visibility and publishing capabilities on Google Play,” with more details coming later this year. 

	

Today’s other announcement is a “requirement for app developers to make log-ins faster and safer during device transfers.” This will be done through a Zero-Tap Sign-In standard that requires apps to “automatically restore a user’s sign-in state when they move from one Android device to another with the Android Restore Credentials API.”

This API ensures that when a user opens your app on their new Android device for the very first time, they are instantly recognized and securely signed in without additional taps. 

This will be required by Google Play starting in April 2027. Games are currently exempt, with more plans coming next year.

fullText:

Nothing OS 5.0 won’t fully launch in a public release until October. The company’s version of Android 17 packs in a few important changes to the UI, like homescreen transparency updates and new lockscreen clock faces. The phones will also support Google’s new 3D emoji and get new apps.

But the current beta build, while technically available, has already caused some issues. According to Nothing co-founder Akis Evangelidis, who posted an update on Twitter/X, the company is seeing an “overwhelming response” to the new beta release. He says some users are seeing error messages related to the new beta.

It sounds like users are getting these errors when trying to download the update, not with the installation itself. Bugs are common with beta software, but this seems more like a bandwidth issue on Nothing’s part than any Phone (3) downloading the Android 17 update.

fullText:
Apple TV has picked up a new comedy series, Small Prophets, for its streaming service in an atypical fashion for the streamer. Rather than commission the project upfront, Apple has bought out the worldwide rights for the series a few months after the show debuted in the UK to record ratings.

Small Prophets was the biggest new scripted series launch for the BBC this year, and Apple will be hoping to replicate its success around the world. It streams on Apple TV starting October 7.

Thanks to this deal, the series will now stream worldwide on Apple TV. Most markets, including the US, will get to watch it on October 7, and it will come to Apple TV in the UK next year. (It is currently exclusive to BBC iPlayer in Britain.)

With a sensibility very much in the vein of other light and airy Apple comedies, like the currently airing Ted Lasso, Small Prophets will fit in well as part of Apple’s catalog. 

The show follows Michael Sleep, whose girlfriend Clea vanished seven years prior. He discovers an old alchemy recipe to create homunculi, which can seemingly predict the future and help him learn about exactly what happened to Clea. 

This acquisition play represents the first time Apple has bought out an English-language title in this manner. It has done similar deals in the past for international content, like the French-Japanese drama Drops of God. It shows Apple’s continuing flexibility and willingness to strike deals, as it builds out an ever-growing content library for the service.

title: Lachy Groom backs Indian startup aiming to keep aircraft aloft for a year
snippet: Founded by a 20-year-old, Alteon is developing autonomous aircraft that hopes to harvest wind energy to stay aloft for several months.
fullText:
Prominent solo investor Lachy Groom has backed a Bengaluru startup attempting an ambitious feat: keeping an aircraft in the sky for more than a year by harvesting energy from ocean winds.

Alteon, founded by 20-year-old Samay Sanghvi, announced Tuesday that it raised $2.5 million in a pre-seed round led by Groom, with participation from Together Fund, to develop autonomous aircraft inspired by dynamic soaring, a technique albatrosses use to extract energy from the wind. Groom decided he wanted to invest within the first 30 minutes of their first meeting, Sanghvi told TechCrunch.

Conventional aircraft need to carry the fuel or battery power required for a flight. Alteon is trying to break that limitation by designing its small, fixed-wing autonomous aircraft that can extract energy from wind shear above the ocean through dynamic soaring — a maneuver in which an aircraft repeatedly moves between layers of air traveling at different speeds.

“Once you build airplanes that can stay in the air for more than a year, there are millions of things you can do with them,” Sanghvi told TechCrunch. Alteon plans to initially use the aircraft for maritime surveillance, giving governments real-time visibility into activity in their waters.

The initial plan is to build an aircraft with around a three-meter-wingspan that will fly close to the ocean’s surface, climb, and turn through faster-moving air, and repeat the cycle to gain energy from the wind. Eventually, Alteon plans to use its propellers as turbines to convert some of that energy into electricity and recharge its onboard batteries, Sanghvi said.

Alteon Founder Samay SanghviImage Credits:Alteon

However, the startup has not yet demonstrated that its aircraft can actually sustain flight using energy harvested through dynamic soaring. It did complete a recent of its test of its autonomous flight system over the Bay of Bengal in which the aircraft autonomously completed seven O-shaped cycles at more than 62 miles per hour, flying within one meter of the water’s surface.

Alteon’s next major milestone will be what Sanghvi calls “energy-neutral dynamic soaring.” This would allow the aircraft to fly continuously with its propulsion switched off, extracting enough energy from the wind to remain aloft.

Dr. Gabriel Bousquet, a Silicon Valley-based aerospace and robotics engineer who researched dynamic soaring during his PhD at MIT, called Alteon’s low-altitude flight over water a “promising first result.” But he noted that the harder challenge will be proving that the aircraft can reliably extract enough energy from real-world winds to sustain flight for extended periods.

Flying low enough to harvest that energy safely is particularly difficult, Bousquet told TechCrunch, as the aircraft would have to contend with turbulence, waves, spray, rain, and changing light conditions while continuously sensing and reacting to a moving ocean surface.

Dr. Bharath Swaminathan, who earned his PhD from IIT Madras studying the stability of dynamic soaring, said the underlying physics is well established and called Alteon’s effort commendable. Keeping an aircraft airborne for several days using dynamic soaring would itself be “a very big step, and a big achievement,” he told TechCrunch.

Swaminathan, however, added that while large-scale wind conditions may be predictable, local wind shear and turbulence can vary substantially, complicating an aircraft’s ability to continuously extract energy from the wind. Some of those challenges, he suggested, may only emerge through real-world flight testing.

Groom acknowledged the technical risk behind the bet. “Ambitious problems are always going to come with risks,” he told TechCrunch. “For me, it came down to believing Samay and the Alteon team are the ones to figure them out.”

Sanghvi began working on what would become Alteon straight out of high school in 2023, learning to build aircraft by making — and crashing — radio-controlled models before developing early prototypes. He formally founded Alteon in 2025 and received early backing from Emergent Ventures and 1517.

Alteon now has a team of 20 in Bengaluru and operates from a 10,000-square-foot facility. The startup is building four to five aircraft a week for testing and has conducted more than 200 test flights in the past 30 days, Sanghvi said.

title: This video experiment perfectly illustrates my frustration with iPhone Cinematic mode
snippet: I recently observed that Apple appeared to have abandoned Cinematic mode, and a video experiment perfectly illustrates my frustration at this fact. That’s not because the feature is bad, but rather that it comes so close to being good enough for real-life use that it’s hard to see why Apple hasn’t taken advantage of the massive increases in power between the iPhone 13 on which it launched and the latest iPhones. Let me show you what I mean … more…
fullText:
I recently observed that Apple appeared to have abandoned Cinematic mode, and a video experiment perfectly illustrates my frustration at this fact.

That’s not because the feature is bad, but rather that it comes so close to being good enough for real-life use that it’s hard to see why Apple hasn’t taken advantage of the massive increases in power between the iPhone 13 on which it launched and the latest iPhones. Let me show you what I mean … 

I said previously that I understood why Apple hasn’t made updating it a priority, but also argued that it should do so to encourage future videographers and filmmakers – especially teenagers who may not have access to any other camera kit.

A friend of mine uses a smartphone to interview complete strangers passing by on the street, and somehow succeeds in having them open up in ways you could never imagine. I decided to turn the tables and put him on the stool and to likewise film using a smartphone, in this case my iPhone 16 Pro Max.

I wanted to see how well Cinematic mode could cope with a relatively simple challenge: a person in the foreground with around 25 feet of separation from railings behind him, and probably close to a thousand feet to the O2 on the opposite side of the Thames. Additionally, he would be sat on a stool, meaning rather limited movement.

The answer was … so close yet so far. The overall look is good, but there are visible halos between CK’s legs and the railings, the O2 pylons come into focus some of the time when he moves his head in front of them, and the river occasionally comes into focus when he opens his arms:

To be fair, CK argues that the average person viewing the video isn’t going to see the problem. If they are neither a filmmaker nor a techie familiar with the way the feature works, they probably won’t even notice the issues, and it won’t bother them if they do. I suspect he may well be right.

But it does bother me, and I think anyone with even amateur filmmaking ambitions will share my frustration – and that’s precisely the target market for the feature.

As I said at the outset, my frustration isn’t because the feature is bad, but rather because I genuinely believe that it could be dramatically better if Apple took full advantage of the power of the current generation of iPhone chips and the neural processing capabilities they possess. Indeed, I would expect a properly updated version of Cinematic mode to be able to cope with significantly more challenging environments than this.

Do you agree with my assessment, and would you like Apple to show cinematic mode some love? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

fullText:
John Higgins

 

is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

Just a few weeks ago the only midrange OLED options available were from LG and Samsung. But after Sony officially announced the Bravia 6 last week, Roku has now launched its first-ever OLED TV — the Roku Pro Series — which will be followed by the step-up Pro Series LX next month.

The Roku Pro Series has a 120Hz panel, four HDMI 2.1 ports, and supports Dolby Vision and HDR10 Plus. It also has auto low latency mode, FreeSync Premium, and VRR for gaming. A backlit Roku remote is included, and a remote finder button on the TV helps locate it when misplaced. The Pro Series LX is about twice as bright as the regular Pro Series, supports 144Hz VRR, and has a polarizer to reduce reflections. And of course both TV series use the Roku operating system.

The Pro Series is exclusive to Amazon for 2026, available now, and comes in 55- and 65-inch sizes starting at $999. The Pro Series LX will be available in October in 55 inches for $1,299 and 65 inches for $1,599.

title: Android still dominates global smartphone sales; Google’s Pixel 10a shines in one country
snippet: Updated data shows that, yep, Android is still the dominant force in the global smartphone market, but country-by-country breakdowns would hint otherwise – and Google’s Pixel series really only breaks into the conversation in one country, too. more…
fullText:
Updated data shows that, yep, Android is still the dominant force in the global smartphone market, but country-by-country breakdowns would hint otherwise – and Google’s Pixel series really only breaks into the conversation in one country, too.

Counterpoint Research published a breakdown of global smartphone OS share, measured by sales, with Android taking the win by a mile. On the global scale, Android makes up about 75% of smartphone sales compared to iOS, which makes up 20%. The last 5% is Huawei’s HarmonyOS. Q2 2026’s numbers aren’t that different from the same time last year, with Android down from 79%, ceding 4% to Apple and 1% to Huawei.

Counterpoint Research

The report brings out that the popularity of the Galaxy S26 series, the Ultra in particular, helped in “mitigating” Android’s overall decline amid RAMageddon’s impact on the market. 

Android’s sales share fell 4% YoY in Q2 2026 to 75%, as competition from iOS and HarmonyOS intensified. The Samsung Galaxy S26 series performed better than its predecessor, mitigating the overall decline in Android’s share. Chinese Android OEMs are shifting their focus to higher-value devices and scaling back activity in the entry-level segment to navigate RAM shortages and rising costs.

Meanwhile, another Counterpoint report breaks down the top five best-selling smartphones in major markets across the globe in Q2 2025, with most markets seeing Apple’s iPhone 17 series up on top. That includes, Japan, which stands out on the list because right behind the iPhone 17 and iPhone 17E is Google’s Pixel 10a, the only place Google stands out in all of this talk about top-selling phones. The Pixel 10a made up 7% of Japan’s smartphone sales in Q2, continuing a trend of popularity among Google’s budget-conscious Pixel in the region. It’s also noteworthy as the Pixel 9a didn’t make the same list this time last year.

title: FTC accuses Amazon of running a ‘secret ad surcharge scheme’ in new lawsuit
snippet: Amazon is facing a new lawsuit from the FTC and 22 states for allegedly secretly charging businesses more for advertising.
fullText:
Amazon is facing a new lawsuit from the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and 22 states, which accuse the company of secretly charging businesses more for advertising on its platform.

The lawsuit, filed Monday, claims Amazon spent more than seven years quietly increasing the prices advertisers paid through its online ad auctions. According to the complaint, the alleged practice affected more than 1 million brands and sellers and may have generated tens of billions of dollars in additional revenue for Amazon.

The 22 states joining the FTC are Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Vermont, and Washington.

The lawsuit centers on Amazon’s Sponsored Products ads, Sponsored Brands ads, and Display ads that run alongside its search results. According to the FTC, Amazon told more than 500,000 small and medium-sized businesses that it ran a “second-price” auction where the winning advertiser would pay just one cent more than the next-highest bid, rather than the full amount of their own bid. Because businesses believed they’d only ever pay slightly more than the runner-up, they had an incentive to bid high, trusting the system would keep their actual costs in check.

But the FTC alleges that starting in 2019, Amazon made a “surreptitious” change without telling advertisers. It added a hidden surcharge that Amazon internally called a “soft reserve price,” and used what one internal document called an “invented auction participant” — a fake bidder, basically — to push prices higher than true competition would have produced. 

The complaint alleges this amounted to a shill bid: rather than the price coming from a real competing advertiser, Amazon was manufacturing a higher number for advertisers to beat. As a result, the FTC claims Amazon charged Sponsored Products advertisers their own full winning bid close to 80% of the time — effectively turning what was marketed as a second-price auction into a first-price one.

The FTC claims Amazon made this change because it wanted more advertising revenue, and kept it hidden because disclosing it could have led advertisers to lower their bids, which would have cut into that revenue. 

The company generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year. 

In a blog post, Amazon described the FTC’s lawsuit as “misguided,” arguing that the complaint “fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate.”

The company added that its auctions evaluate billions of bids across different placements and formats, so prices naturally vary, and advertisers are “properly” informed about the pricing system.
