title: Apple cleared for the second time to pursue documents from federal agencies in antitrust case
snippet: Special Master Jose Linares has rejected the DOJ’s request to reconsider his decision allowing Apple to seek documents from 14 separate government agencies in the antitrust case against the company. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Special Master Jose Linares has rejected the DOJ’s request to reconsider his decision allowing Apple to seek documents from 14 separate government agencies in the antitrust case against the company. Here are the details.

A bit of background

One of Apple’s defense strategies in the antitrust lawsuit the DOJ brought against the company involves the US government’s own use of its products.

Apple’s basic argument is that some of the practices challenged by the DOJ are, in fact, legitimate security and privacy safeguards. Hoping to support that defense, Apple wants to examine how federal agencies evaluate security and privacy when setting smartphone policies and making purchasing decisions.

To that end, Apple has been seeking documents from the following 14 agencies:

Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)

Department of Commerce

Department of Homeland Security

Department of Defense

Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)

Federal Trade Commission (FTC)

General Services Administration

Department of Labor

National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)

National Security Agency (NSA)

Office of the Director of National Intelligence

Office of Management and Budget

Office of Personnel Management

Department of State

Following Apple’s initial request to force these agencies to turn over the documents, the DOJ objected. The dispute was then referred to Special Master Jose Linares for a ruling.

Last month, Linares granted Apple’s request, prompting the DOJ to file a motion for reconsideration. It argued that he had applied the wrong legal standard, that Apple’s requests were unduly burdensome and disproportionate, and that the documents sought had limited relevance to the case.

Apple then filed an opposition arguing that the DOJ’s motion “failed at every level” and refuting the department’s arguments point by point.

Linares has now issued his new decision, concluding that “none of [the DOJ’s] arguments in support of its application for reconsideration are persuasive,” and leaving his original ruling in place.

Apple cleared to seek documents

The new decision states:

The Special Master concludes that none of Plaintiff’s arguments in support of its application for reconsideration are persuasive.

It adds that Linares saw “no reason, persuasive or otherwise, to reverse course at this point,” adding that “Federal Agencies, in this case, (are) part of the United States for purposes of party discovery.”

From the decision:

Plaintiff tries to split hairs by asserting that, under Rule 45 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, “a non-party to litigation is afforded greater protection from discovery than a party.” […] Thus, Plaintiff concludes that the Special Master’s Order and Opinion rests on flawed reasoning since it did not reference or incorporate Rule 45 into the analysis.

The Special Master is familiar with Rule 45 and the different standards applicable to third-party discovery. A quick review of the Special Master’s Opinion and Order reveals that Plaintiff is simply incorrect. Indeed, the Special Master detailed how this dispute arose in detail. […]. A review of that portion of the Opinion and Order reveals that Plaintiff itself is the reason why Defendant had to issue the subpoenas in the first place.

The document goes on to explain that Linares considered the 14 federal agencies to be part of the United States, rather than third parties entitled to the additional protections that normally apply under Rule 45:

[…] the discovery sought here from the specific Federal Agencies is appropriate party discovery because “the definition of the ‘United States’ also includes agencies that inform the policies, rules, and regulations the executive branch sets.” (Order at 6 (emphasis in original and added)). Thus, Plaintiff is wrong that the Special Master needed to perform a Rule 45 third-party burden analysis here. […]

The document also says the DOJ “misunderstands the legal framework applicable to this dispute,” while criticizing its assertion that the requested information had “minimal” relevance as being made “without citation to any support.”

As a result, Apple is once again cleared to seek the documents from the 14 federal agencies.

title: I’ve Run the Numbers and Read the Tea Leaves. Here’s When I Expect Apple to Release iOS 27
snippet: I think I know the exact date Apple will release iOS 27.
fullText:
Apple announced iOS 27 at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June, and the tech giant has since released multiple beta versions of the software. The betas have brought Siri AI and a handful of other features to the iPhones of developers and beta testers, and you can expect many of those capabilities to land on your iPhone soon. 

Perhaps sooner than you expect.

So far, Apple has only said that it will release the update to the general public this fall, which isn’t the most helpful timeframe. If we look at past Apple events in September and earlier iOS releases, though, we can see a release pattern. Apple usually releases iOS versions a few days after the company’s September event, and I expect that trend to hold this year.

Based on those trends and a little psychic peering, I believe Apple will release iOS 27 on Monday, Sept. 14.

I was right about iOS 26’s release in 2025, iOS 18’s release in 2024 and iOS 17’s release in 2023, so I’m sure I can keep this streak going. But if you want the full breakdown of how I arrived at that date, here’s how.

How my iOS 27 release date math works

Usually Apple releases the next iOS update soon after the September event and the company is set to hold its “Surprise and shine” event on Wednesday, Sept. 9. While Apple doesn’t usually announce the release of iOS versions, the company has been pretty consistent with its release schedule over the years. 

After most of Apple’s September events, the company releases the next iOS within a week. In 2025, for example, Apple’s event was held on Sept. 9 and the company released iOS 26 on Sept. 15. And in 2024 Apple’s event was held on Sept. 9 and iOS 18 was released seven days later on Sept. 16.

There’s only been one year over the past decade where it took longer than a week for Apple to release the next iOS version – 2019. That year, Apple released the next iOS version nine days after its September event.

In that same timeframe, most of the iOS releases were either five, six or seven days after the September event. Apple has also released the past five iOS versions on the Monday following its September events. This could be the new norm, with Apple releasing future iOS versions on the Monday after its September events moving forward. 

So it’s most likely that Apple will release iOS 27 on the following Monday, Sept. 14.

For more on iOS 27, here are my first impressions of the beta and what to know about iOS 27 before Apple brings it to your device later this year.

title: Polymarket reportedly raises $300 million from Donald Trump Jr.’s investment fund
snippet: The firm, 1789 Capital, led the funding round that reportedly will total around $1 billion.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

4:41 PM PDT · August 31, 2026

Image Credits:Omar Marques/SOPA Images/LightRocket / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

The popular prediction market Polymarket has raised $300 million from 1789 Capital as part of a new funding round totaling around $1 billion, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing unnamed sources.

1789 Capital, an investment fund in which Donald Trump Jr. is a partner, previously invested $200 million in the prediction site. The firm has funded other controversial tech-related projects, including the Enhanced Games, the so-called “steroid Olympics” founded by veterans of various tech companies.

TechCrunch has reached out to Polymarket for comment.

Prediction markets have come under increased regulatory scrutiny, as many state governments seek to institute new rules around how (or even if) the sites can be used by residents. There are at least 20 states engaged in litigation against prediction sites over sports wagers offered on those sites.

The federal government, meanwhile, has frequently sought to defend the prediction industry from state regulation. The Trump administration has argued that the sole regulator of the industry should be the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), not state governments. The CFTC has sued at least nine states over their attempts to regulate the industry.

A coalition of 44 state attorneys general recently signed a letter arguing that the CFTC does not have the authority to regulate sports-related wagers on prediction sites.

The New York Times has reported that Donald Trump Jr. recently appeared at an event involving conservative state attorneys general, where he described the prediction industry as already having “robust oversight” and characterized prediction sites as a tool “overseen by federal officials, not state attorneys general.”

title: iOS 27’s Passwords app adds powerful feature that can save you time

fullText:
Among the many Apple Intelligence features coming in iOS 27, the Passwords app is getting an especially powerful one: the ability to automatically change your passwords for you.

Passwords app in iOS 27 can fix compromised logins on your behalf, powered by Apple Intelligence

A new era of Apple Intelligence is at the heart of the forthcoming iOS 27 and companion software updates. One powerful new AI feature involves the Apple Passwords app.

Passwords launched two years ago as a dedicated hub for logins, 2FA codes, Wi-Fi credentials, passkeys, and more.

The app has always shown you if passwords in your database are problematic in some way. For example, if your password has been spotted in a data leak, or is used across multiple accounts, the Passwords app notifies you of that.

But until now, you’ve always needed to manually fix those problematic logins.

In iOS 27 though, Apple says that in many cases, its new agentic AI feature can change the passwords for you. Per its website:

Fix passwords with a tap. The Passwords app alerts you to weak or compromised passwords and can update them on your behalf without the hassle.

Thanks to this feature, you can always ensure that your logins are secure and use strong passwords, but with minimal hassle or time spent on your part.

iOS 27 is currently in beta, and will launch to all users in the next few weeks. The new Passwords feature is expected to ship in iOS 27.0, but its availability in the beta has been inconsistent, so it might get pushed into iOS 27.1.

title: Yearn for the Tern: Apple Has a New Daddy
snippet: John Ternus takes the helm of a $4 trillion tech giant, but it comes with challenges as Apple faces down the RAM shortage, AI launch delays and the foldable phone market.
fullText:
John Ternus took over as Apple CEO on Tuesday, succeeding Tim Cook after serving as the company’s senior vice president of hardware engineering. His first day comes just over a week before the annual iPhone launch event on Sept. 9.

Under Cook, Apple became a $4 trillion company with an impressive, world-changing lineup of tech products, including every iPhone from 2012’s iPhone 5 onward, the Apple Watch, the AirPods, the Vision Pro and the HomePod, and services including Apple Music, Apple TV Plus and Apple Fitness Plus. 

But what exactly is Ternus walking into? There are major challenges ahead, driven by the global RAM shortage, increasing smartphone competition and Apple’s struggles to keep up with the artificial intelligence race.

Farewell to Tim Cook

Cook, who took over as CEO two months before Apple co-founder Steve Jobs passed away in 2011, reportedly held a farewell party at Apple Park last weekend to cap off his 15 years at the helm of the company. Around 200 people — mostly Apple employees, but also Cook’s partner and the band OneRepublic — attended the party, according to The Information, citing unnamed sources.

Ternus reportedly spoke at the event, along with Steve Jobs’ widow, Laurene Powell Jobs; Apple’s former COO, Jeff Williams; and head of Apple Services and Health, Eddy Cue.

According to that report, anonymous sources have said the transition from Cook to Ternus should be one of continuity rather than upheaval, with many things expected to stay the same.

During his final earnings call as CEO in July, Cook praised Ternus, saying, “There is no better person to take the helm of the company.” He also called Ternus “brilliant and wonderful and capable” in his farewell note as Apple CEO on Monday.

“Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does, and I could not be more excited for his leadership,” Cook wrote this week.

With Ternus as CEO, Cook now serves as executive chair of Apple. Keeping him on in a senior role means Cook will still have influence over where Ternus decides to take Apple, and he could continue to be particularly influential with the current presidential administration, with which he’s fostered a good working relationship.

The Ternus takeover: Who is the new Apple CEO?

Ternus joined the tech giant back in 2001 as part of the product design team, having earned a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Pennsylvania and working as a mechanical engineer at Virtual Research Systems.

Rising through the ranks at Apple over 25 years, he became a VP of hardware engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021. Ternus worked across many flagship devices, including the iPad, AirPods, iPhone, Apple Watch and, most recently, the MacBook Neo. Apple also credits Ternus with improving device durability by incorporting 3D-printed titanium in the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and creating a recycled aluminum compound.

Ternus was last year tipped to be the frontrunner in the race to succeed Cook, and at 51, he’s around the same age Cook was when he took over as Apple CEO.

In Apple’s April announcement, Cook said Ternus “has the mind of an engineer, the soul of an innovator and the heart to lead with integrity and with honor.”

“Having spent almost my entire career at Apple, I have been lucky to have worked under Steve Jobs and to have had Tim Cook as my mentor,” Ternus said at the time.

IDC Worldwide Device Trackers senior research director Nabila Popal told CNET that she is “genuinely excited for Apple to go full circle and bring a products guy to lead Apple in this next phase, with an innovative lineup of interesting devices rumored to launch in the first few years of his leadership.”

The first two CEOs of Apple were likewise “products guys” — Michael Scott ran a semiconductor company, and Mike Markkula was an electrical engineer — so the choice of Ternus is a return to Apple’s roots.

The state of Apple in 2026: What is Ternus inheriting?

Bloomberg/Getty Images

His takeover comes just over a week before Apple unveils its next set of products, likely including the long-rumored foldable iPhone and the iPhone 18 lineup — but there are challenges ahead, even with a highly anticipated product launch.

One major test for Ternus will be the prices for the next iPhone, which are likely to have a higher price tag due to the ongoing global RAM shortage caused by the rapid expansion of AI tools. In June, Apple raised prices on over a dozen products across iPads, Macs and home devices.

“The September launch will be an important first test for John Ternus as CEO,” Counterpoint Research principal analyst Yang Wang told CNET. “A premium-focused lineup could strengthen Apple’s product mix, but it also increases the risk if pricing moves too far ahead of consumer demand.”

Most phones released this year have seen $100 bumps, including the Samsung Galaxy S26 line, while a few higher-end models have gone up $200 over their predecessors. Counterpoint projects the iPhone 18 lineup to see a price increase of $200-$250 per phone compared to the iPhone 17 lineup, “with high-spec models potentially seeing price hikes even beyond the range.”

Rumors suggest a standard iPhone 18 won’t be part of the lineup next week, instead launching in the spring alongside a potential iPhone 18E. This could extend the shelf life of the current iPhone 17, which is still seeing “strong demand” in 2026, according to Counterpoint Research. Typically, Apple discounts its previous model by $100 when a new iPhone is announced; if there’s no new base model, Apple can keep the iPhone 17 at its full price.

“Ternus knows the hardware organization very well, but the challenge will be balancing product ambition with affordability and launch execution,” Wang said, adding that he expects Samsung to overtake Apple for the global smartphone lead by the end of 2026.

The chip shortage across DRAM and NAND flash, which are needed for phones but are being gobbled up by AI data centers, is real. But there has been some criticism that tech giants are not shielding customers from chipflation despite seeing record sales; Apple, for instance, raked in roughly $109 billion in net sales and reported almost $30 billion in net income during the previous quarter.

At the end of August, analyst firm IDC said smartphone shipments are set for a record 17% drop this year due to the memory crisis, with NAND and DRAM costs up 300% compared to last year.

“The components that make AI possible are the same ones in short supply, and their cost is being passed straight through to the shelf,” IDC vice president for worldwide client devices Francisco Jeronimo wrote on Aug. 26. “Average selling prices are up 27.6% this year and will keep rising well into 2027. The era of the cheap smartphone has ended.”

According to IDC, “foldables remain the only silver lining.”

Could a foldable revitalize the iPhone?

Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

Apple is late to the foldable phone game, assuming it finally launches one next week. Samsung is now on its eighth generation of foldable phones, with the recent launch of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Flip 8, which follow the company’s first foldable phone in 2019. There are also competitor folding phones such as Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold, Motorola’s Razr Fold and other Chinese options from Oppo, OnePlus and Huawei.

IDC is predicting “rapid growth” in the foldable phones market thanks to Apple’s expected entry into the sector. It forecasts Apple will ship more than 17 million foldable iPhones by next year, snatching 40% of the folding phone market share, potentially making it the dominant force over Samsung, Google and Huawei.

Counterpoint Research has a little less glaze on its folding iPhone predictions, saying that with an expected price tag of $2,200 — IDC predicts $2,550 — its customer base will be limited and shipments will account for just 3% of all iPhones.

“The device is likely to target affluent early adopters and existing Pro Max users looking for something between an iPhone and an iPad,” Wang told CNET. “This is less about competing directly with Samsung or Google and more about creating a new top tier within Apple’s own portfolio.”

Wang said Apple’s late entry into the foldable market is unlikely to be a disadvantage, though, given the supply chain is now more mature and there have been technological improvements in hinge design, display creases and durability.

It’s important to remember that a foldable isn’t guaranteed success, however. CNET’s survey of more than 2,600 adults last month found that 75% were not interested in a foldable iPhone, and that most would only want to spend around $781 on an Apple foldable phone — which is $48 less than a base-model iPhone 17.

Under Cook, Apple expanded from two iPhone models a year to five; the addition of a foldable phone would bring the total to six iPhone models just a week into Ternus’ new role. It wouldn’t necessarily matter whether the iPhone Fold is a hit if it does the job of expanding the iPhone price range well beyond $2,000 to appeal to higher-end buyers.

Regardless of how much work was put into the folding iPhone before he took over, Ternus will own the success or failure of Apple’s purported foldable. But it’s not the only area he’s tasked with bringing Apple back into the lead.

Where does AI fit into Apple’s future?

Apple is also behind on AI, even settling a lawsuit over the lack of AI features in its previous iPhones after overpromising and underdelivering. While Siri AI remained under development, Apple inked deals with OpenAI to use ChatGPT on iPhones and with Google to leverage Gemini to expand Siri.

After years of delays, Apple finally unveiled Siri AI and improved Apple Intelligence during its annual software conference, WWDC, in June. It now has its own app, a fresh design, customized voice options, more accurate dictation, better context for improved suggestions, integrated writing tools, the ability to pull info from your messages, emails and other apps and what Apple calls “broad world knowledge.” 

Visual Intelligence has been rolled into a new Siri mode in the camera app, including the ability to identify family and friends in photos by name and to search screenshots for products online.

Siri AI is expected to launch later this year in beta, possibly timed with the release of the new iPhones, so for now, it remains to be seen whether Apple can truly compete with AI giants such as Google and OpenAI.

One of the biggest industry pressures facing Ternus will be remedying this and ensuring a smooth rollout of AI features in Apple’s phones and Macs to match its competitors. However, a CNET survey found that AI isn’t a major motivator for people to upgrade their phones, and there are also rising concerns from consumers about how much water and power AI data centers are sucking up and what kind of privacy implications there are when AI is integrated into everything. 

By choosing a hardware-focused CEO, however, Apple may be signaling that it wants to focus on devices over AI — unless a move into physical AI is imminent for the tech giant.

“The biggest challenge for Apple as Ternus takes over is how to keep the company relevant in the age of AI,” Popal told CNET. “But what will be crucial is whether the level of innovation can keep up with consumer expectations as the world is rapidly shifting into an unknown AI era, where how we interact with our devices is changing, and for the moment, it is increasingly looking like we are moving towards a more voice-powered interface than touch.”

While a smart glasses announcement next week is unlikely, we’re expecting a refresh of Apple’s AirPods, and rumors are swirling around AirPods with AI-powered cameras that can use Visual Intelligence to improve Siri’s context about your surroundings and give better suggestions and answers. It’s part of a slate of unreleased products that are powered by Siri AI.

But there are privacy implications in being tracked and monitored by tiny, hidden cameras embedded in earbuds, too.

“It’s hard not to see this upcoming product launch as Apple simply chasing the AI arms race rather than genuinely listening to customer needs,” said Lee Elliott, chief product officer at Compare and Recycle, a tech recycling comparison site, in a statement last week. “Camera-equipped earphones will certainly be storing far more personal data, including images, locations and environmental data.”

Announcing new products always comes with an air of excitement, but in the age of AI everywhere and RAM shortages driving global price hikes, the main challenge for Ternus as he steps into the CEO role will likely be balancing privacy, AI hesitancy and pricing against launching one more thing.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Corinne Reichert
						

						

							Senior Editor						
					

											

				

											Corinne Reichert (she/her) grew up in Sydney, Australia and moved to California in 2019. She holds degrees in law and communications, and currently writes news, analysis and features for CNET across the topics of electric vehicles, broadband networks, mobile devices, big tech, artificial intelligence, home technology and entertainment. In her spare time, she watches soccer games and F1 races, and goes to Disneyland as often as possible.

title: Four advantages iPhone 18 Pro will have over the iPhone Ultra
snippet: Apple is about to unveil its flagship new iPhones: iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra. Price will be an obvious advantage for the Pro line, but here are several other ways iPhone 18 Pro will have an edge over the more expensive Ultra model. more…
fullText:
Apple is about to unveil its flagship new iPhones: iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra. Price will be an obvious advantage for the Pro line, but here are several other ways iPhone 18 Pro will have an edge over the more expensive Ultra model.

#1: Main camera with variable aperture

iPhone 18 Pro is rumored to get big changes to its Main camera, including a variable aperture upgrade. And expectations are that iPhone Ultra won’t get the feature.

Variable aperture has been rumored for a while, but we still don’t know exactly how Apple plans to implement it. It could provide big improvements to Portrait mode and offer new levels of control over depth of field. Low-light photography could similarly get a big boost.

The components required to enable variable aperture are expected to be larger than the current Main camera. As a result, it’s believed that the ultra-thin iPhone Ultra will miss out.

#2: Longer battery life on Pro Max

iPhone Ultra should offer solid battery life, per regulatory leaks. But the Pro line—specifically iPhone 18 Pro Max—will still offer the best battery life in an iPhone.

iPhone 18 Pro Max is reportedly getting a 10% larger physical battery than iPhone 17 Pro Max. It will also benefit from efficiency gains in the A20 Pro and C2 chips. As a result, battery life should easily be the best ever in an iPhone.

With the unique form factor of a foldable, it’s hard to judge iPhone Ultra’s battery life based on specs alone. But the ultra-thin design and smaller physical battery will no doubt keep it from matching iPhone 18 Pro Max.

#3: Face ID

For the first time in years, a flagship new iPhone model won’t offer Face ID. Instead, iPhone Ultra will be limited to Touch ID.

iPhone 18 Pro, meanwhile, will stick with the Face ID system that’s been around for nearly a decade now.

Apple reportedly couldn’t make enough room in the thin iPhone Ultra design for the Face ID components. Proper support would have required double the components, too: one set for the outer display, and another for the inner one. So in the authentication department, iPhone 18 Pro will have a clear advantage.

#4: Telephoto camera

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will continue being the only models that offer a Telephoto camera. iPhone Ultra will have Main and Ultra Wide cameras, but no Telephoto for optical zoom.

This could be a big differentiator for a lot of users who rely on the Telephoto. Especially because Apple is rumored to make its Telephoto camera even better this year with a larger aperture.

If you’re looking for the best camera system, iPhone 18 Pro will be the no-brainer choice.

Bonus: Traditional iPhone experience

This isn’t technically a feature, but it’s worth mentioning. For many users, iPhone 18 Pro offering a ‘traditional’ iPhone experience will be an advantage.

	

iPhone Ultra will be unique from every model that’s come before it. The outer and inner displays will have sizes and shapes that feel a bit foreign to the iPhone. And the need to fold and unfold rather than using just a single display could take some adjusting.

The iPhone is a beloved product in its current form factor. And while foldables definitely have a lot of fans, I suspect for the average consumer who might never read 9to5Mac, iPhone 18 Pro having a traditional iPhone design will be an advantage for many.

Which new iPhone model are you planning to buy this fall? Let us know in the comments.

title: Apple has announced 11 new products in 2026 so far, with more coming soon
snippet: Apple has moved through 2026 in bursts. First came a new AirTag in January, followed by a packed March launch cycle and two major Mac updates in August. Add everything up, and Apple has announced 11 new hardware products this year, with its biggest event still ahead. more…
fullText:
Apple has moved through 2026 in bursts. First came a new AirTag in January, followed by a packed March launch cycle and two major Mac updates in August. Add everything up, and Apple has announced 11 new hardware products this year, with its biggest event still ahead.

AirTag 2 started the year

Apple’s first new hardware of 2026 arrived on January 26 with the second-generation AirTag.

AirTag 2 uses Apple’s second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, extending Precision Finding range by up to 50%. It also offers a longer Bluetooth range, a louder speaker, and Precision Finding from compatible Apple Watch models.

Apple kept pricing unchanged at $29 for one AirTag or $99 for a four-pack. Amazon currently lists each for $24 and $79.99, respectively.

Eight new products in March

March delivered the bulk of Apple’s 2026 hardware announcements so far, with eight products unveiled during the month.

The month started with the $599 iPhone 17e. Apple doubled the starting storage to 256GB while adding the A19 chip, C1X modem, MagSafe, and a new soft pink color.

Apple also introduced the M4 iPad Air in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes. It gained 12GB of memory alongside Apple’s C1X cellular modem and N1 wireless chip.

One day later, Apple announced four more products: the M5 MacBook Air, M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro, an updated Studio Display, and the all-new Studio Display XDR.

Apple followed that lineup with the all-new MacBook Neo on March 4. The $699 laptop uses the A18 Pro chip and became Apple’s most affordable Mac notebook.

Finally, Apple returned on March 16 with AirPods Max 2. The H2 chip powers improved noise cancellation, Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Live Translation, and other features previously unavailable on AirPods Max.

Mac mini and Mac Studio announced

Apple’s latest hardware announcements came on August 25.

The updated Mac mini offers either Apple’s new M6 chip or M5 Pro. Both configurations gain faster storage, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and standard 2.5Gb Ethernet. Pricing starts at $899.

Apple also unveiled a new Mac Studio powered by M5 Max or M5 Ultra. The highest-end configuration supports up to 512GB of unified memory.

Both Macs are available to pre-order now and will begin reaching customers on September 22.

Much more could be weeks away

title: Galaxy S26 FE is $699 with last year’s specs, Android 17, and a few new features
snippet: Debuting with a higher price tag and effectively the same spec sheet, the Galaxy S26 FE might as well be a poster child for living through “RAMageddon.” more…
fullText:
Debuting with a higher price tag and effectively the same spec sheet, the Galaxy S26 FE might as well be a poster child for living through “RAMageddon.”

Samsung has just unveiled its new Galaxy S26 FE, with the “Fan Edition” device offering more or less an identical set of specs compared to last year’s Galaxy S25 FE – 6.7-inch FHD+ AMOLED display, Exynos 2500 chip, 8GB of RAM (128GB/256GB storage), a 4,900 mAh battery with 45W charging, and a triple camera setup on the back comprised of a 50MP main, 12MP ultrawide, and 8MP telephoto (3x). 

Outside of a chipset generation bump, the only new thing this year, at least on paper, is that the Galaxy S26 FE runs Android 17 (One UI 9) out of the box, an update only available otherwise on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 series (and Flip 8). The software packs some added features, too, such as the “My FanCam” that tracks a subject in video for social sharing, new AI features powered by Gemini Omni, and more.

Samsung has also updated the design this year, with a new camera bump look that’s closer to the rest of the Galaxy S26 series. It also comes in “Blueberry,” “Graphite,” and “Pistachio” colorways.

	

It’s a tough sell, to say the least, given Galaxy S25 FE launched for $50 less last year, and currently sells for as little as $500 outright through some carriers and retailers. But that’s just life during “RAMageddon,” ain’t it?

Galaxy S26 FE will be available on September 4.

fullText:
Executive Summary, Day One

📁 Inbox 5:05AM

To: Ternus, John <jternus@apple.com>

Reply-to: CEO-transition-team@apple.com

Welcome to your first day as CEO! Hopefully you’re finding your new office spacious and comfortable. If you have trouble with any of the doors just ping us — being a Jony Ive design, you won’t find anything as unsightly as a door handle here!

Today’s memo includes a summary of the business, broken out by division. The day’s schedule is also attached; please note that the Apple Intelligence team needed to delay the new Siri discussion until a later date, but they promise they’re “for real” this time.

Hardware

Everything is in hand for the upcoming phone launches. We don’t anticipate the price hikes will have much impact on sales, since nobody in the US knows how much they really pay for their phone anyway. The team agrees that calling the camera on the upcoming AirPods a “sensor” would make it less creepy and is moving forward with that terminology. Morale on the Vision Pro team after their move to the basement is somewhat low, but we’ve scheduled a virtual offsite for them in Tahiti that we think will help.

Services

Our new EU app store rules go into effect in exactly one month. We’ve compiled a simplified explainer breaking down how much commission app developers will pay and which companies can operate alternative app stores into an easy-to-parse, 300-page PDF (see attached). This does mean that our services revenue will take a hit, but on the bright side, we just rolled out ads in Maps to juice the numbers.

Despite the setbacks, services is still our best bet for growth since we, well, ran out of people to sell iPhones to. It might even become a bigger business than the iPhone someday. That could fundamentally change the kind of company Apple is — a hardware guy in charge of a services company? Or will a services company pivot back to hardware under a new CEO? Striking that balance without frustrating customers remains an ongoing challenge. Take a hint from your predecessor: Ted Lasso is so lovable nobody noticed that we raised Apple TV prices again.

Software

The good news is that the updated Liquid Glass design is polling with higher approval ratings than last year. The bad news is that Brussels is still mad at us for holding back new Siri in Europe, Google’s kind of eating our lunch in the EU, and app developers are still unhappy with the new commission structure. We were, uh, not winning any popularity contests with app developers to start with, so this may be something to consider.

Operation Smarter Siri Take Two has been a success, and we’re finally back in the AI game. Unfortunately, in the time that passed since Smarter Siri The First Try, AI became deeply unfashionable. But it kind of works in our favor; we can let Meta and Google take the heat on building out all those data centers (pun intended?) while we cajole app developers into using app intents so Siri can actually do stuff. Once again, see above point about developers.

Side note: Alan Dye was seen near campus holding a sign that reads “Liquid Glass is good, actually” but security handled it.

Special Projects

The car lab has transitioned nicely into the new AI wearable testing / smart home facility. There’s a little conflict between the sleep tracking team and the Beats team over the noise level in the test house, but we gave the sleepers some AirPods with noise cancellation, which should resolve the issue. Oh, and the Pope has expressed interest in trying the AI Siri pin. He loves his Apple Watch, and apparently His Holiness would like a screen-free way to brush up on his White Sox trivia in his downtime.

At least Meta is giving us a pretty low hurdle to clear, right?

Sentiment among beta testers on the smart glasses is a tad low — “Creepy as F—” tends to come up a lot in feedback. The team remains confident and has some anti-creep modifications planned. At least Meta is giving us a pretty low hurdle to clear, right? This might be a segment to pay attention to after you’re settled in. There are growing concerns in how we can maintain our stance on privacy while putting cameras on people’s ears and in their glasses.

Upcoming Key Activities

Just a reminder of some upcoming events: The team is gathering tomorrow night for drinks celebrating Phil’s not-quite-retirement. Tim’s goodbye drinks thing is tonight, and as a parting gift, he wants to review last quarter’s production numbers, for old time’s sake. He really does have a different idea of “fun,” doesn’t he? He’ll be heading to DC immediately after; President Trump has requested his help troubleshooting an issue with his iPad. Also, you’ll find Kate’s retirement party on your calendar. And Jennifer’s retirement party. That’s a lot of exits, huh? At least Craig still insists he isn’t going anywhere. We’re keeping a close eye on him anyway.

Of course, there’s your big debut as CEO coming up next week. Rehearsals have looked great — you’ve really been studying the Cook-ian “Good Morning!” bellow. Sure, investors will be looking for any sign of weakness. And a big price hike just as we’re introducing a new boss isn’t great timing. There’s a lot hinging on this keynote, you could say.

If there’s any way we can help make your first day better, don’t hesitate. Just relax and remember you’re running the world’s most profitable company in a time of political uncertainty, a historic supply chain crisis, unprecedented governmental scrutiny, and top executive shuffling. No pressure, Big J! You got this. Time to surprise and shine!

title: Google Maps has renamed ‘Lake America’ for users in the US
snippet: Following an executive order late last week, Google Maps has updated its label for “Lake Ontario” to “Lake America.” more…
fullText:
Following an executive order late last week, Google Maps has updated its label for “Lake Ontario” to “Lake America.”

If you are located within the United States, viewing “Lake Ontario” via Google Maps will now show the name “Lake America,” following last week’s executive order. 

Google, in a brief blog post, confirms that users in Canada will continue to see only “Lake Ontario” while users in other parts of the world will see “Lake Ontario (Lake America).” This can also be seen using a VPN.

From the United States
From Canada

Google continues to cite a policy in which it updates location names based on local government data; in this case, the US GNIS, where the name has been updated as of August 27 by the Department of the Interior following Trump’s order. Google referred to this same policy in February 2025 when it updated Maps to show “Gulf of America.”

	
	

Canada has confirmed that it will not be updating the name from “Lake Ontario,” with Prime Minister Mark Carney stating that “the name is more than 400 years ​old, predating ​both the Confederation of Canada ‌and ⁠the Declaration of Independence of the United States of ​America.” Carney added that the name comes “from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.'”

Notably, competitor MapQuest has directly said it will not change the name, instead building out a name generator that allows users to create their own new names for the lake, mocking the change. Apple Maps is not yet showing the name either. Apple changed “Gulf of America” within a day or two of Google back in February, though.

Steep backlash pushed Google to limit new reviews of “Gulf of America” in 2025, but the same limitation has yet to be placed on “Lake America,” we observed in testing.

AirPods 5 expected to launch at September 9 event in two models, but no cameras

Apple’s biggest event of the year is happening next week on September 9. Alongside new iPhones, Apple Watch models, and likely Home products, AirPods 5 are also expected to debut. 

AirPods 4 launched in 2024, and historically Apple has had two- or three-year gaps between generations. AirPods launched in 2016, AirPods 2 in 2019, AirPods 3 in 2021, and AirPods 4 in 2024. So from a timing standpoint, a launch this year more or less fits the pattern.

[Apple is] planning to debut fresh AirPods as early as the September product launch event. The rollout will include new AirPods 5, an update to Apple’s entry-level earbuds, the people said. with Active Noise Cancellation

without ANC

title: AT&T Lawsuit Says Charter Is Misleading Customers With ‘Fiber-Powered’ Claims
snippet: The new lawsuit is centered around what a fiber connection really means for customers.
fullText:
Two of the country’s largest internet service providers are going to court over the definition of “fiber.”

AT&T filed a lawsuit against Charter on Friday, alleging that its marketing of “fiber-powered” internet is misleading customers. The argument centers around an ad campaign from Charter, which sells home internet under the brand name Spectrum. 

Fiber is widely considered the gold standard for home internet. Fiber used to be the only connection type capable of delivering symmetrical upload and download speeds, but the latest DOCSIS 4.0 technology allows cable providers to transmit symmetrical speeds after upgrading their networks. On Spectrum’s cable plans, typical upload speeds top out at 40Mbps, while download speeds exceed 1,000Mbps. I always advise readers to go with a fiber provider whenever it’s available. 

Over the past couple of years, cable internet providers have increasingly tried to capitalize on that fiber cache. It’s technically true that Spectrum provides “fiber-powered” internet. Like all cable ISPs, Spectrum uses fiber-optic cables — thin glass strands that carry data through light signals — for the vast majority of its network. But it switches to copper coaxial cables in most cases to travel the proverbial last mile to your home. Fiber providers like AT&T, on the other hand, run the fiber connection all the way to the jack in your wall. 

Many cable companies are in the process of upgrading that last mile to fiber. Spectrum currently reports to the Federal Communications Commission that 2.3% of US households have access to its fiber plans, while 29.9% can get its cable plans. 

“We don’t think customers should have to be telecom experts or squint at the fine print to know what they’re buying,” an AT&T representative told me in an email. “When internet is marketed as fiber, customers deserve 100% fiber all the way to their home.”

I spot-checked a handful of addresses on Spectrum’s website in Dallas, where AT&T is filing its lawsuit, and some of them did return fiber plans. According to FCC data, which is self-reported by ISPs, Spectrum covers around 608,000 households in Dallas, while AT&T covers almost 495,000. 

This isn’t the first time Charter has been chided for passing itself off as a fiber provider. In March, Spectrum agreed to modify its “fiber-powered” statements after AT&T brought a challenge through the BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division.

Spectrum’s advertising describes its service as “fiber-powered” but notes in the fine print that it’s connected via coaxial lines.Spectrum/Screenshot by CNET

As a part of that challenge, Spectrum agreed to “clearly and conspicuously” disclose that its “fiber-powered internet services are not delivered to customers’ homes over a fiber-to-the-home infrastructure.” The fine print on Spectrum’s internet page notes that the connection to the premises is delivered via coaxial lines.

Charter did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Counterpoint: iPhone 17 topped worldwide smartphone sales during Q2
snippet: In a report published today, Counterpoint Research says Apple once again secured five spots among the world’s 10 best-selling smartphones during the second quarter of 2026. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a report published today, Counterpoint Research says Apple once again secured five spots among the world’s 10 best-selling smartphones during the second quarter of 2026. Here are the details.

MagSafe and higher storage help push iPhone 17e into top 10

Over the past several months, there has been no shortage of reports pointing to the success of the iPhone 17 line, particularly as most of Apple’s closest competitors raised prices due to the ongoing component shortage.

Just days ago, Counterpoint published three reports showing that Apple bucked a broader downward trend across several regions, posting growth in both shipments and sales.

Today, the firm published a new report claiming that the iPhone 17 was the world’s best-selling smartphone during Q2 2026, accounting for 6% of global smartphone unit sales.

Apple also secured the second and third spots with the iPhone 17 Pro Max and iPhone 17 Pro, respectively, while the iPhone 17e ranked seventh and the iPhone 16 came in tenth. The latter had topped the year-ago ranking with a 4% share.

Samsung was the only other manufacturer to make the top 10, with the Galaxy S26 Ultra 5G in fourth, followed by the Galaxy A07 4G in fifth, the Galaxy A17 5G in sixth, the Galaxy A17 4G in eighth, and the Galaxy S26 5G in ninth.

Counterpoint also said that the top 10 best-selling smartphones contributed to 26% of overall sales, up 2% year-over-year.

Here’s Counterpoint Research’s Senior Analyst Karn Chauhan on Apple’s performance for the quarter:

Apple’s unit sales grew 5% YoY despite a broader market decline. iPhone sales increased across India, Japan, and the MEA, and nearly doubled in South Korea in Q2 2026, driven by the iPhone 17 series. The base iPhone 17 model remained the best-selling smartphone during the quarter, supported by significant upgrades that narrowed the gap with the Pro models. Meanwhile, strong premium demand drove the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max sales, aided by trade-in programs, promotions, and accessible financing options that improved affordability. Rising smartphone prices also pushed consumers towards the higher-end segments, further strengthening Apple’s competitive position.

title: Galaxy S27 leaks reveal a design that Samsung just won’t kill
snippet: Whether you’re a fan of the Galaxy S27 Ultra’s new camera design or not, Samsung is ditching the cohesive design that has tied its Galaxy S models together last year. The Galaxy S27 looks nothing like the Galaxy S27 Ultra, according to these latest leaks. more…
fullText:
Whether you’re a fan of the Galaxy S27 Ultra’s new camera design or not, Samsung is ditching the cohesive design that has tied its Galaxy S models together last year. The Galaxy S27 looks nothing like the Galaxy S27 Ultra, according to these latest leaks.

What appear to be official-looking render images of the Galaxy S27’s design have appeared online, showing every nook and cranny of the new base model (via Android Headlines). The only part about this leak that might be off-putting is the fact that the Galaxy S27 looks nothing like the Galaxy S27 Ultra, which recently leaked in a similar fashion

The Ultra model has a new camera design similar to what Apple designed into the iPhone 17 Pro. The camera “pateau” expands the island we usually see around the lenses to span the entire rear width of the phone. For whatever reason, Samsung did it, whether it’s for Qi2.2 or less wobble when the phone lies face-up, the point is that it’s a major shift. Don’t get your hopes up for Qi2 magnets, though.

The Galaxy S27, however, won’t be much of a shift, or even a nudge.

	

The leak indicates Samsung’s Galaxy S27 will have nearly identical dimensions and design to the Galaxy S26, save for a fraction of a millimeter in each direction. It will bring another 6.3-inch display to users who want the smaller model of Samsung’s Galaxy S line.

Inside, there’s a question as to what the company plans on putting at the helm. It could be a top-tier Snapdragon SoC, or it could be Samsung’s own silicon. Storage configurations are also a mystery, for now. With the price of RAM jumping further and further, the possibility of another price hike and less RAM is on the table. The Galaxy S27 Ultra could come with a price increase, according to previous reports. The same is very possible for the Galaxy S26.

It’s interesting to see Samsung making such a big change to the Galaxy S27 Ultra while keeping the more affordable options essentially unchanged in design since the Galaxy S23, even. Even when the Galaxy S26 Edge was reportedly set for a debut as the middle-ground option, Samsung had to kill it in favor of – you guessed it – the same design that was leaked today. It just won’t die.

The Galaxy S27 is expected to launch at the beginning of next year.

title: Apple reveals ‘shocking evidence’ from ex-employee’s MacBook in OpenAI suit
snippet: Apple has filed a new document in its ongoing lawsuit against OpenAI as it continues to push for expedited discovery. In today’s filing, Apple says that it has new “shocking evidence” based on early forensic inspection of a laptop used by former engineer Chang Liu. more…
fullText:
Apple has filed a new document in its ongoing lawsuit against OpenAI as it continues to push for expedited discovery. In today’s filing, Apple says that it has new “shocking evidence” based on early forensic inspection of a laptop used by former engineer Chang Liu.

Apple first filed the lawsuit in July, accusing ex-employees of stealing trade secrets for the benefit of OpenAI. It moved for a preliminary injunction a few weeks later, while also asking the court to expedite discovery, including early document production and depositions of key OpenAI employees and executives. Apple again emphasized the need for expedited discovery last week. OpenAI has called for dismissal. 

As covered before, Chang Liu is one of the parties named in Apple’s lawsuit. Liu was a senior system electrical engineer at Apple who left the company for OpenAI in January. The lawsuit alleges that Liu exploited a security bug to download confidential engineering files after leaving.

In today’s filing, Apple says that Liu’s lawyers recently handed over his MacBook that he used after leaving Apple. According to Apple, an “initial forensic analysis” of that MacBook revealed four things, quoted from Apple’s filing:

Mr. Liu not only downloaded a confidential Apple circuit schematic but also used it in his work at OpenAI;

Far from his unauthorized access to Apple’s third-party cloud storage being unknown to him, Mr. Liu and others at OpenAI were well-aware of that access;

Mr. Liu, upon learning of Apple’s internal investigation of him, sent instructions for destroying evidence to an OpenAI colleague who confirmed she would comply; and

Mr. Liu used a tool in his work at OpenAI that has the same name as an internal Apple engineering application used for Apple development work.

Apple alleges that Liu ran a simulation in March using the circuit schematic file in LTspice, an electrical engineering tool. In messages from around that time, Liu said his AI “agent” learned to run LTspice and review the results.

Apple argues that when trade secret information is fed into an AI agent or model that learns from it, that learning “may create irreversible and continually propagating uses of the trade secret.”

Apple says the defendants decided not to inspect the laptop and instead chose to “advance theories that the device’s data disproves.” 

Additionally, Apple learned about Liu’s use of the schematic because he used it on a Mac mini which later synced via iCloud to the MacBook he took from Apple. Apple now also wants access to that Mac mini. 

This “shocking evidence” is yet another point in favor of expedited discovery in the case, Apple says:

“This shocking evidence—which Defendants chose to ignore despite its availability—demonstrates why Apple urgently needs expedited discovery. The MacBook represents the very limited information Defendants provided so far (and only after weeks of delay), and shows Apple is not conducting ‘fishing expeditions’ but that its trade secrets are being used and evidence is being destroyed.”

title: Chrome’s Android navigation bar redesign has too much chrome
snippet: I quite like how Chrome for Android’s main interface has essentially remained the same since 2012. The consistency is refreshing as everything else on my phone changes. While I’m open to modernization, the latest attempt at a redesign suffers from too much chrome. more…
fullText:
I quite like how Chrome for Android’s main interface has essentially remained the same since 2012. The consistency is refreshing as everything else on my phone changes. While I’m open to modernization, the latest attempt at a redesign suffers from too much chrome.

When the browser launched in 2008, the name was meant to signify speed and a minimal graphical user interface, or chrome. On Android, that philosophy has persisted with just an address bar at the top or bottom of the screen. That text field can be flanked by various buttons, but the most minimal state consists of just the tab switcher and three-dot overflow menu. Over the years, Google has just refreshed these elements while keeping the placement unchanged.

Old vs. new

The upcoming redesign once again adds a secondary toolbar at the bottom of the screen that has buttons for your homepage (which can be disabled), Gemini, new tab, and the tab switcher. This lets Google add a dedicated back button to the left of the Omnibox, while the toolbar shortcut is now placed inside.

	

Google was close to launching a similar revamp in 2020, but ultimately abandoned it because “mainstream users” found it “disorienting.”

I don’t mind the Gemini shortcut, and think giving people a dedicated new tab button is a good idea. That was my toolbar shortcut of choice for ages, and Google is now showing a share button by default next to the URL. (Tip: Long-press on the address bar to quickly copy links.)

If you keep the address bar at the top, this interface is perfectly fine. However, as a bottom bar user, the stacked interface elements are just so thick. When you first scroll down a page and the interface auto-hides, it really hammers home how much web content Chrome is covering.

Things become downright ridiculous when viewing Tab Groups. Having three rows stacked on top of one another looks comical and makes your screen feel infinitely smaller. To me, this interface is not usable, and I’ve forced myself back to the top address bar. 

Simply making the bottom toolbar thinner would help a great deal. It would salvage this redesign and let Google stick to the browser’s namesake design.

This navigation bar redesign is slowly rolling out to the stable channel. It’s not clear whether Google has committed to this interface, but I hope it changes before launch. Ideally, Google would preserve the original interface as an option, but that seems unlikely.

title: iPhone Ultra release timing: Here’s what the latest reporting says
snippet: Apple will unveil its foldable iPhone Ultra next week at the September event, but it’s unclear exactly when the new model will ship to users. Here’s what to expect per the latest reporting. more…
fullText:
Apple will unveil its foldable iPhone Ultra next week at the September event, but it’s unclear exactly when the new model will ship to users. Here’s what to expect per the latest reporting.

iPhone Ultra is likely to ship in September, but with very limited availability per reporting

Next week, Apple will debut its first ever foldable iPhone model: the iPhone Ultra. 

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are coming too, expected to go on sale later that week ahead of wide availability September 18.

But even though iPhone Ultra will be announced at the same event, it’s still unclear if Apple’s foldable model will actually ship to users at the same time as iPhone 18 Pro.

There have been countless reports over the last several months regarding the launch timing for iPhone Ultra. Fortunately, the most recent reporting is optimistic that we’ll see the device ship in September—albeit with limited supply.

Earlier this month, Weibo leaker Fixed Focus Digital said supply will be “extremely limited” at launch, but per his sources in the supply chain, there’s no evidence of a delay past September.

Similarly, a July report in Cailian News Agency referenced conversations with Apple supply chain sources. “They said that there was no change in the delivery time date in September, denying rumors of product postponement.” ChannelNews Australia was another recent source saying the device would be available in September, at least in the US.

Looking further back though, the story changes. 

Ming Chi-Kuo predicted earlier in the summer that iPhone Ultra will follow a similar strategy to the iPhone X in 2017. Meaning it could be announced in September but ship later in the fall. Macworld heard a similar plan from its sources.

And back in April, Nikkei Asia stirred a lot of buzz by reporting the foldable could be delayed several months into 2027. Mark Gurman at Bloomberg refuted that report though, saying the device was still “on track” for September.

iPhone Ultra release timing: wrap-up

In summary, the more recent reporting indicates that iPhone Ultra will indeed ship in September. It might be available in very limited territories and quantities, but early adopters should be able to buy it soon.

When do you expect iPhone Ultra to launch? Let us know in the comments.

title: Nothing’s Android 17 update debuts this week with redesigns, new apps, 3D emoji [Gallery]
snippet: Nothing has announced Nothing OS 5.0, its Android 17 update, which will start rolling out in October with some redesigned UI elements, more AI features, new apps, and support for Google’s 3D emoji too. more…
fullText:
Nothing has announced Nothing OS 5.0, its Android 17 update, which will start rolling out in October with some redesigned UI elements, more AI features, new apps, and support for Google’s 3D emoji too.

Nothing OS 5.0 isn’t a complete overhaul, but it’s not a small update either. Rolling out starting in October, the Android 17-based update brings a host of new updates throughout. This includes various UI updates, including Pixel-like transparency/blur on some homescreen widgets and in apps like Nothing Gallery, lockscreen clock faces, batch editing on the homescreen, new widgets, and even a new dedicated app for Nothing’s Glyph features.

A condensed version of the changelog for Nothing OS 5.0 follows:

New font throughout the system UI

Status bar animations for feedback when changing connection modes, more

Camera app: Updated icons, QR links now stay fixed on screen once recognized

Nothing Gallery gets better sorting, album organization options

New homescreen personalization and batch editing

Lockscreen gets two new clocks and more color theming

Wallpapers add more depth and blur effects

New widgets: “Away Time” to show time not using your phone, “Collector” for sticker-like widgets on homescreen created from photos

Dedicated Glyph app for light controls, features, etc

Bluetooth controls upgraded in Quick Settings

Essential AI updates:

Essential Voice now shows a live preview of text while processing voice-to-text output

“Smart Collections” automatically sort Essential Space content

Essential Apps can now be built through an app on your Nothing Phone

Separate Quick Settings & Notification panels (optional)

Yellow AI privacy indicator

Noto 3D emoji (also available on Pixel 11)

Nothing says to expect Nothing OS 5.0 (Android 17) to start rolling out to Phone (3) in “mid-October,” with the rest of its supported devices – dating back to Phone (2a) – being updated through mid-January. 

	

Open Beta builds will be available starting tomorrow, August 26, starting on Phone (3) and expanding to other devices in the coming weeks. Somewhat amusingly, Phone (4b) is second-to-last in line, despite being the company’s newest smartphone.

title: Google’s hyper-personalized ‘Dreambeans’ feed is now free to test
snippet: Dreambeans is an experimental app from Google Labs that will “proactively dream up personalized daily stories.” After previously requiring a subscription, Dreambeans is now available for free Google Accounts in the US to test. more…
fullText:
Dreambeans is an experimental app from Google Labs that will “proactively dream up personalized daily stories.” After previously requiring a subscription, Dreambeans is now available for free Google Accounts in the US to test.

Dreambeans is very much like a hyper-personalized Google Now or Discover feed. Like the Gemini app and AI Mode, it uses Google’s Personal Intelligence system to learn your interests by looking at your Gmail, Google Photos, Calendar, Workspace, Search history, and YouTube. During setup, you can choose which apps Dreambeans can access.

Workspace supplies ground-truth transaction data like receipts and upcoming flights

Photos provides the visual memories and insights about you and the people in your life

YouTube identifies your active hobbies

Search detects your budding interests

By combining all these unique signals, Dreambeans can proactively generate rich and highly customized daily visual stories.

The app suggests topics to explore, things to try, places to visit, and interesting events. New stories arrive every morning.

Instead of using stock imagery, each Dreambeans story is accompanied by Nano Banana 2-generated artwork that uses an illustrated style. For example, if Dreambeans recommends a hike, you might see yourself and a group of friends at that location.

	

Tapping on a story lets you see a longer description. In the same example, you’ll get trail details, specific places to stop, what to wear, and timing recommendations. Dreambeans will link to trail guide content on the web. There’s also an “Ask anything” chat experience to get more information.

You can leave feedback by tapping the heart or downvoting, while the chat interface allows you to provide more details. “Tune your feed” lets you tell Dreambeans what you “want more stories about” and what it should never show.

The name combines two ideas at the heart of the app. The “dream” is how the app works overnight to find meaning in the content overload across your connected apps. It then distills what it finds into “beans” – a fresh collection of stories brewed for you each morning.

In June, it was just available for Google AI Ultra subscribers, with Google expanding to AI Pro earlier this month. The setup process “requires up to a day to build your first set of stories.” 

It remains to be seen how Dreambeans will graduate from Google Labs. The experience it offers today is largely standalone, with Daily Brief in the Gemini app possibly benefiting from a more visual experience. 

Dreambeans is available on Android and iOS in the US.

title: What is the ‘Android Pulse’ app that just appeared in Google Play Store updates? [U]
snippet: On Saturday morning, you might have noticed an app called “Android Pulse” appearing in the list of available Google Play updates. more…
fullText:
On Saturday morning, you might have noticed an app called “Android Pulse” appearing in the list of available Google Play updates.

Update 8/25: In a statement today, Google explained that “Android Pulse is a Google system service.” 

Google system services updates make your Android devices more secure and reliable, and give you new and useful features.

—Google spokesperson

The app’s appearance in the Play Store was accidental, and Google has “pushed an update so users will now see it in their settings.” It now appears in the usual list alongside Google Play services and Android System Intelligence. On Pixel, go to Settings app > Google services > All services > Privacy & security > System services to check.

Original 8/22: Instead of an application icon, there’s just a blank square. Opening the Play Store listing does reveal it’s a first-party Google app meant for “Defining anomalies for debugging” rather than anything malicious.

	

com.google.android.apps.pulse

Google adds: “This app facilitates rule distribution for anomaly detection in critical system resource consumption by the Android operating system and installed applications.”

What does Android Pulse do?

That’s not a very user-friendly description, but our interpretation is that this service — which does not have an interface you can access — helps with software diagnostics for the OS itself and any installed apps. The “critical system resource consumption” could be a reference to battery, CPU, or memory usage.

This application is already installed on our Pixel devices, and it’s just referred to as “Pulse” in system Settings. The App info page also reveals a heart rate-inspired icon in green (as seen in the cover image above).

Let us know if you’re seeing this app or update on non-Pixel devices

	

According to APKMirror, this app has existed since March, with seven previous builds. The Play Store notes over 10 million downloads.

However, today is the first time it appears to have surfaced in the Play Store as an update you can manually install. It’s curious that Google did not use its dedicated System Services approach to update this kind of app.

In short, “Android Pulse” is a Google app that’s okay to have on your phone.

title: The Fitbit Air would be S-tier if anyone made a band half as decent as Whoop’s
snippet: The Fitbit Air is being touted as a fantastic fitness tracker, but I don’t think its worth has quite yet been proven. Google-made and third-party bands do not make for a comfortable experience, and competitive trackers blow it out of the water in terms of fit. more…
fullText:
The Fitbit Air is being touted as a fantastic fitness tracker, but I don’t think its worth has quite yet been proven. Google-made and third-party bands do not make for a comfortable experience, and competitive trackers blow it out of the water in terms of fit.

I was a little late to jump on the Fitbit Air bandwagon. For some time, I grew accustomed to using an Oura Ring, as reviews in the past have showcased. The form factor is wonderful, and the newest model, the Oura Ring 5, gives users a more comfortable experience because it’s so much thinner. I haven’t used the newest edition, and instead walked myself back to fitness bands like the Whoop 4.0. I still had the hardware even with yet another new model available, but I find it works just fine.

It’s expensive, though.

For $25/month, you get the basics as Whoop sets them. Whoop sets them high, to be fair, just like Oura does. Elevated metrics and studies bump the price up, but Google has proven that a good health suite can be free with hardware. We’ve documented the Google Health app well, and it sets a fantastic bar for a subscription-free service. Of course, you can always opt into the AI coach powered by Gemini for an added $10/month.

	

What bothers me after using the Fitbit Air for a few weeks is the comfort, or lack thereof. Coming from Whoop’s knitted bands and clasp system, I find the Fitbit Air to be difficult to forget about. That’s what you want, after all – a band that goes unnoticed minutes after putting it on. The main point of contact should feel better than it does, and these proprietary bands just don’t do it for me.

They feel stiff, don’t seem to breathe very well, and have given me the first taste of contact dermatitis that I’ve ever experienced on a wearable. Maybe it was tighter than it needed to be, or maybe these bands don’t have any give with the natural swelling and contracting your skin does throughout the day.

The Google-made bands I’ve tried just don’t have any serviceable stretch. Granted, I haven’t used the more expensive Elevated or Active band because of the added cost at around $50. Just the Special Edition Stephen Curry band and the default Performance Loop band have lived on my pebble. Still, compared to the included strap that comes with Whoop’s fitness trackers, Google’s hardware severely lags behind.

I’d love to have a band option with a similar clasp system – something set-and-forget. By comparison, the Fitbit Air Performance Loop band requires a bit too much patience for something I need to remove and put back on daily.

The market is already flooded with Fitbit Air adapters that let you use the hardware with Whoop’s bands, but that’s literally just a band-aid. It completely negates the reason the Air exists – minimal footprint on an 18mm strap. On size alone, the Fitbit Air beats Whoop hands down.

You could make the overarching argument that the Fitbit Air’s affordable price is made possible because the sensor’s enclosure isn’t made from more premium materials, like aluminum or titanium – the latter might be overkill. That feels more like an excuse, since even additional band options don’t seem to be as premium.

The third-party landscape doesn’t offer much better than Google does, yet.

Your best bet is finding Fitbit Air bands from Amazon and even dropshipping websites like Aliexpress. Google’s good-faith move to make Fitbit Air band designs available ‘s enclosure design available hasn’t yet paid off. I haven’t found many creative or premium designs hit online stores, and if there are shops selling Fitbit Air bands, they’re generally getting them from Aliexpress.

Hopefully, that changes and we begin to see premium bands with unique hardware from accessory companies with solid track records – looking at you, UAG, Nomad, and Spigen. Those are just a couple of companies to call out, but the option is there for an accessories brand to develop some good options.

All that’s to say the Google Fitbit Air is a solid fitness tracker with an affordable price, but it would be S-tier with more comfortable bands.

title: Apple Maps still shows Lake Ontario as Google Maps changes name
snippet: The latest development in the trade war Trump started with Canada is an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America. Google Maps has updated the name, though what you see depends on which country you are in, with only US users seeing Lake America. Apple Maps has so far stuck to the real name … more…
fullText:
The latest development in the trade war Trump started with Canada is an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America. Google Maps has updated the name, though what you see depends on which country you are in, with only US users seeing Lake America. Apple Maps has so far stuck to the real name … 

Lake Ontario is this year’s rerun of the Gulf of Mexico. Trump last year signed an executive order stating that the latter would be renamed to Gulf of America, and has now signed another saying that the smallest of the Great Lakes will be renamed Lake America.

Canada and most of the rest of the world has responded with amusement and mockery. Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a new billboard on the shoreline of the lake reading “Lake Ontario. Now and always.”

Google Maps has updated its naming, with the label depending on where you are based:

US users: Lake America

Canadian users: Lake Ontario

Rest of the world: Lake Ontario (Lake America)

This mirrors the approach the company took with the Gulf of Mexico. Associated Press cites a Google blog post stating that its policy is to use the names assigned by the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).

So far, however, Apple Maps has stuck to Lake Ontario, including for US users. Whether it too will compromise as it did for the Gulf of Mexico remains to be seen. The company normally tries to avoid political flak, and has often taken the decision to appease the Trump administration, but with a new CEO, this may or may not change.

title: Apple’s next iPad mini is almost ready, here’s what to expect
snippet: Apple has a lot in store for this fall, headlined by the iPhone Ultra and iPhone 18 Pro launching next month. Apple is also working on a new iPad mini, and a new report today suggests it’s coming in October. more…
fullText:
Apple has a lot in store for this fall, headlined by the iPhone Ultra and iPhone 18 Pro launching next month. Apple is also working on a new iPad mini, and a new report today suggests it’s coming in October. 

A new iPad mini is coming soon

In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Mark Gurman reports that the new iPad mini with an OLED screen “should go on sale by the end of October.”

This suggests the new iPad mini won’t be announced at next month’s “Surprise and shine” special event. Instead, Apple will likely announce it separately in October, either via a press release or another event.

As a refresher, here’s what to expect from the next-generation iPad mini:

OLED display

Faster performance, likely powered by the A19 Pro or A20 Pro chip

Better water resistance thanks to a “redesigned casing”

A new vibration-based speaker system

This will mark the first update to the iPad mini in two years. Apple last updated the device in October 2024, adding the A17 Pro chip, Apple Pencil Pro support, and Apple Intelligence compatibility.

The iPad mini’s price increased by $100 earlier this year, from $499 to $599. It’s currently on sale for $569 at Amazon. Whether the next-generation model comes at an even higher price remains to be seen.

Over at 512 Pixels, Stephen Hackett has a great look at the history of the iPad mini and how its role and position in Apple’s lineup has changed over the years. 

I think one of the biggest questions right now is how the foldable iPhone Ultra will impact the market for the iPad mini. The iPhone Ultra essentially offers a 2-in-1 iPhone and iPad mini form factor. Will that cannibalize the standalone iPad mini? I’m doubtful, since I think a lot of people like keeping the iPad and iPhone separate.

title: Apple reportedly considered launching a new Apple Pencil for iPhone Ultra
snippet: Apple’s first foldable iPhone should be making its debut in just over a week. In the development process, Apple was reportedly mulling the idea of launching a new Apple Pencil to use alongside the iPhone Ultra – though it probably won’t make it to market. more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable iPhone should be making its debut in just over a week. In the development process, Apple was reportedly mulling the idea of launching a new Apple Pencil to use alongside the iPhone Ultra – though it probably won’t make it to market.

This news comes from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, who wants to make it very clear that this pencil probably won’t be announced next month. That said, he does detail exactly how it would’ve looked and worked.

It wouldn’t have been the same as Apple Pencils that currently exist for the iPad lineup. It was “stubbier,” to align with the shorter height of the iPhone Ultra. However, similar to Apple Pencils on the iPad, it would’ve magnetically attached to the side for storage and charging.

He notes that it would’ve been awkward to hold while you were using the iPhone Ultra, since it’d stick on the side, versus the iPad where it sticks at the top when you’re in landscape.

He also notes that it likely would’ve made “unsightly marks” on the much more delicate inside screen of the iPhone Ultra.

Ultimately, he reckons that Apple probably isn’t launching this to not conflict with Steve Jobs’ position when launching the original iPhone: “Who wants a stylus?”

I’d still say an Apple Pencil on iPhone Ultra would be rather useful, but it sounds like we won’t have one – at least for the time being.

title: New JBL Cove Wireless Speakers Seem Like a Worthy Sonos Alternative
snippet: The new whole-home Wi-Fi speaker range includes three launch models — X1, P1 and M1 — that start at $230.
fullText:
Sonos is the big name in whole-home wirelesss audio, but JBL is taking another crack at it with its new Cove Wi-Fi speaker line. There are three models at launch: the Cove M1 ($229), Cove P1 ($399) and Cove X1 ($449). The Cove P1 is the only model that’s portable and has a built-in rechargeable battery, though all three speakers feature both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. They’re available for preorder now and ship Sept. 13.

While I haven’t tried the speakers in my own home, I got a taste of them in action at a JBL demo in a swanky loft in New York and was pretty impressed by what I saw and heard. As part of the demo, JBL played each speaker on its own and then linked them together with other Cove speakers and also created a stereo pair using two M1 speakers, which can also be used as rear channels when linked with JBL’s Bar Series MK2 soundbars.

The Cove P1 in white.David Carnoy/CNET

The system works a lot like a Sonos system with speakers grouped by room (or on their own) using the JBL One app for iOS and Android. There’s an automatic self-tuning option, as well as AI Sound Boost technologies that “work to optimize performance based on where and how you listen.” They also have built-in microphones and are Alexa-enabled.  

Needless to say, the X1, which features four tweeters and dual woofers, delivers the biggest, richest sound with the strongest bass performance (it’s comparable to Sonos’ $470 Era 300 speaker). But the M1 and P1 deliver big sound for their size, too, and seem to stack up well against their Sonos counterparts. They’re also priced similarly, though the Sonos speakers cost a little more (for example, the Sonos Move 2 portable speaker costs $499 while the P1 is $399).

The Cove X1 is the current flagship speakerDavid Carnoy/CNET

Back in the day, I liked JBL’s now-discontinued Link Series Wi-Fi speakers, which were released in 2017. They were fairly affordable and sounded decent, but just weren’t as well-designed as Sonos speakers, nor did they have the most user-friendly setup or as polished an app as Sonos’.

At first listen, its new Cove platform seems like a worthy alternative to Sonos, but I’ll have to A/B test those Cove speakers side by side with Sonos’ offerings to really get a sense of how their audio quality measures up. It’ll also be interesting to see where street prices for the Cove speakers land, and whether JBL will offer any discounts on speaker bundles. If they sound as good or even slightly better than their Sonos counterparts and cost less, that would certainly help them find a foothold in the whole-home audio marketplace.
